## DAILY SECURITY BRIEFING

### 1. Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range strikes
Russia continued attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, damaging homes, warehouses, logistics facilities and Kherson’s remaining heat-and-power equipment. Ukraine launched a large drone attack across Russia, claimed a strike on the Yaroslavl refinery and said it critically damaged a Tu-95MS strategic bomber at Engels-2. Civilian casualties were reported on both sides; several military claims remain unverified.

**Why it matters:** Both countries are increasingly targeting strategic assets and infrastructure far behind the front. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also set a goal of expanding Ukrainian long-range strikes from more than 300 to 1,000 drones daily, indicating potential for a substantial escalation.

### 2. CIA-SVR talks revive a sensitive US-Russia backchannel
CIA Director John Ratcliffe met Russian foreign intelligence chief Sergey Naryshkin during an unannounced Moscow visit. Ukraine said Washington briefed it before and after the meetings. Neither side disclosed the agenda, while reports that Ratcliffe warned Moscow against action targeting NATO were denied by President Donald Trump and the Kremlin.

**Why it matters:** The contact provides a direct channel for managing escalation, communicating red lines and potentially discussing Ukraine or prisoner exchanges at a time when formal diplomacy remains limited.

### 3. Russian manpower pressure may increase reliance on North Korea
Western officials assessed that Russia is losing around 6,000 more personnel each month than it recruits, despite adding approximately 1,000 recruits daily. Separately, Ukrainian intelligence warned that Moscow could seek as many as 50,000 additional North Korean troops, while South Korea said Pyongyang was preparing further deployments. No immediate deployment on that scale has been confirmed.

**Why it matters:** A sustained recruitment deficit could constrain Russian operations or increase pressure for another politically risky mobilization. Additional North Korean troops, missiles, ammunition or technical personnel could help Moscow sustain its war of attrition.

### 4. NATO air-defense readiness faces growing strain
Officials cited in reporting said Patriot interceptor stocks in Europe have fallen to critically low levels after heavy use in operations involving Iran. At the same time, Sweden will deploy Gripen fighters and a corvette to support Finland’s surveillance and territorial protection amid concern over drone incursions near NATO’s northern borders.

**Why it matters:** Limited interceptor inventories leave both Ukraine and NATO infrastructure more exposed to ballistic missile attacks. Sweden’s deployment illustrates how allies are compensating for heightened pressure along the Russian frontier.

## WATCH

- **Possible Russian winter escalation:** Reports indicate Moscow may intensify ballistic attacks on Kyiv and Ukrainian energy infrastructure as negotiations remain stalled.
- **North Korean deployments:** Confirmation, scale and role of any additional North Korean personnel sent to support Russia.
- **SCO summit diplomacy:** Planned meetings among Xi Jinping, Narendra Modi, Vladimir Putin and Masoud Pezeshkian could clarify China-Russia coordination, the China-India thaw and Iran’s Eurasian partnerships.

### India expands naval BrahMos deployment

India plans to integrate BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles across more frontline warships by 2030. The navy already deploys BrahMos on about 20 major combatants, while the government has approved 220 extended-range naval missiles capable of striking targets at up to 800 kilometers.

**Why it matters:** Wider deployment would increase India’s ability to attack ships and coastal targets from greater distances while reducing reliance on imported missile types. Following the May 2025 India-Pakistan clashes, the expansion could intensify naval competition and prompt additional Pakistani defensive and offensive investments.

### SCO summit brings major Eurasian powers together

Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are due to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek. Discussions are expected to address regional conflicts, Afghanistan, security cooperation, trade and transport links. A possible Xi-Modi interaction will be closely watched amid tentative efforts to stabilize their disputed border.

**Why it matters:** The summit provides a rare forum connecting China, Russia, India, Pakistan and Iran despite their competing interests. It could indicate whether the recent China-India thaw is durable and whether SCO members can deepen economic coordination amid heightened international pressure and regional instability.

### US, South Korea and Japan reinforce trilateral defense cooperation

The three countries announced the annual Freedom Edge exercise for early September in waters near Jeju Island. The drills are expected to cover maritime missile defense, air defense, anti-submarine warfare and cyber defense. Separately, Washington approved a possible $125 million sale of 103 AIM-9X Block II air-to-air missiles to South Korea.

**Why it matters:** The exercise and proposed missile sale strengthen interoperability and South Korea’s air-defense capabilities against North Korean threats. They also demonstrate continued trilateral cooperation despite Washington’s reduction of other US-South Korean exercises while seeking renewed dialogue with Pyongyang.

### WATCH

- **North Korean response:** Monitor missile tests, military deployments or diplomatic signals in response to Freedom Edge and US arms sales to Seoul.
- **India-Pakistan force posture:** Watch Pakistan’s response to India’s BrahMos expansion and India’s reported efforts to replenish S-400 missile stocks after the May conflict.

## 1. CIA chief opens high-level intelligence channel with Moscow

CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow and met Russian Foreign Intelligence Service chief Sergei Naryshkin. President Vladimir Putin was briefed but did not attend. The agenda remains undisclosed; reports that Ratcliffe warned against Russian action targeting NATO members were disputed by President Donald Trump and the Kremlin. Ukraine said Washington briefed Kyiv before and after the meetings.

**Why it matters:** This was the first known visit by a CIA director to Moscow since 2021. The contact restores a senior-level backchannel that could be used to communicate red lines, manage escalation and discuss Ukraine despite stalled formal diplomacy.

## 2. Russia and Ukraine expand long-range strategic strikes

Russia continued large drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, striking residential, commercial and logistics facilities and causing casualties. Ukraine simultaneously launched a major drone attack across Russia. Kyiv said it hit the Yaroslavl oil refinery and critically damaged a Tu-95MS strategic bomber at Engels-2 airbase; Moscow has not confirmed the bomber claim.

**Why it matters:** Both sides are increasingly targeting assets well behind the front. Russian attacks threaten Ukrainian infrastructure and supply networks, while Ukrainian strikes seek to disrupt Russian fuel supplies and reduce the bomber fleet used to launch cruise missiles.

## 3. Russian manpower pressure increases reliance on North Korea

Western officials estimated that Russian battlefield casualties are exceeding recruitment by about 6,000 personnel a month, despite approximately 1,000 new recruits daily. A further Russian mobilization could carry domestic political and economic costs. Separately, North Korea continues to supply Russia with ammunition, ballistic missiles and specialist personnel. Ukrainian intelligence warned that Moscow could eventually request up to 50,000 additional North Korean troops, although such a deployment has not been confirmed.

**Why it matters:** A sustained personnel deficit could constrain Russian offensive operations or force the Kremlin to mobilize more Russians. Expanded North Korean support could offset some shortages, prolong the war and deepen military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang.

## WATCH

- **European air-defense stocks:** Reported shortages of Patriot interceptors could leave both Ukraine and NATO infrastructure more exposed to Russian ballistic missiles while production expands slowly.
- **Poland’s nuclear-deterrence debate:** The Polish government has rejected hosting allied nuclear warheads, but the presidency and opposition favor keeping that option open, exposing a strategic policy divide on NATO’s eastern flank.

### 1. Hormuz dispute remains central after six months of war

Iran said it is preparing conditions for fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including an end to the regional war, and has discussed a designated shipping channel with Oman. The United States says it controls the strait, has cleared mines and is allowing commercial traffic while blockading Iranian shipping. Efforts to restart negotiations remain stalled, with Washington rejecting a return to the terms of an earlier memorandum.

**Why it matters:** The strait is a critical route for global energy supplies. Continued military enforcement, competing claims of control and the absence of negotiations create risks of escalation, shipping disruption and higher oil prices.

### 2. US and Israel sustain military coordination and regional force posture

US Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach met senior Israeli military leaders to review lessons from their joint campaign against Iran and discuss further cooperation. Although major strikes have slowed, the United States continues to maintain dozens of aircraft and other forces in the region, while shifting emphasis toward blockading Iranian ports and shipping and applying economic pressure.

**Why it matters:** The continuing US deployment preserves the ability to resume large-scale operations quickly. Deeper operational coordination with Israel also signals that the conflict remains active despite the reduced pace of airstrikes.

### 3. Iran signals military expansion as regional security alignments evolve

Iran’s Defense Ministry said arms production has more than doubled since the 12-day war and claimed advances in missiles, drones, counter-drone systems and strategic stockpiles. Separately, Iranian officials acknowledged informal proposals for dialogue with members of the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, while denying receipt of a formal invitation to join.

**Why it matters:** Iran is presenting military resilience and increased domestic production as the basis for renewed deterrence. At the same time, exploratory engagement with the Mecca pact could influence whether the emerging grouping develops as an anti-Iran coalition or a broader regional security framework.

## WATCH

- **US-Iran diplomacy:** Monitor whether mediation by Qatar and Oman produces agreed terms for Hormuz or renewed nuclear and war-ending negotiations.
- **Threats against Persian-language media:** Iran’s warning that overseas outlets could become military targets has prompted US and Czech concern and could create new security or diplomatic confrontations.

### Hypersonic weapons investment accelerates

US defence technology company Castelion announced a $1 billion financing round to expand production of its Blackbeard hypersonic missile, develop a longer-range strike system and advance air and missile defence technologies. It plans substantial additional investment at its Project Ranger manufacturing campus in New Mexico and is targeting Blackbeard fielding in 2027.

**Why it matters:** The funding could expand US capacity to manufacture hypersonic weapons at scale and reflects growing private-capital involvement in defence production. Castelion says it has secured more than $500 million in US military contracts over the past 18 months.

### US attack submarine overhaul reaches milestone

The Virginia-class attack submarine USS *North Carolina* left dry dock at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard on schedule after restoration and modernisation work. It has moved to a pier-side berth for further work before returning to service.

**Why it matters:** Virginia-class submarines support anti-submarine warfare, strike, intelligence and special operations missions. Timely completion of maintenance is important for sustaining US undersea availability in the Indo-Pacific, although the submarine has not yet returned to operational service.

### US states tighten scrutiny of data-centre expansion

Texas Governor Greg Abbott criticised data-centre companies over public backlash, while Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro imposed stricter conditions, including ending fast-track permits and requiring binding community commitments. Concerns include electricity costs, power demand and local infrastructure burdens, despite tax revenue, employment and investment benefits.

**Why it matters:** Greater state-level regulation could affect the pace, location and cost of US artificial-intelligence infrastructure development. The shift also highlights growing tension between strategic AI investment and public concerns over energy prices and community impacts.

### WATCH

- **Blackbeard production:** Monitor whether Castelion converts new financing into manufacturing capacity and meets its 2027 fielding target.
- **Data-centre regulation:** Watch for similar restrictions in other states and any effects on electricity markets, project delays or investment relocation.

articles.title: Deal, warning or spy swap? What Russian media are saying about the CIA chief’s Moscow visit
articles.body:
Deal, warning or spy swap? What Russian media are saying about the CIA chief’s Moscow visit
On August 25, it was not so much the CIA director as a ready-made story that landed in Moscow: a hulking C-17 military transport, several hours away from the cameras, secret meetings, and a return flight via Riga. By Friday, barely any more facts had emerged. SVR head Sergey Naryshkin confirmed that the talks concerned matters within the intelligence services’ purview, calling the field “sensitive and highly specialized.” Ratcliffe did not meet with Vladimir Putin, but the Russian president was briefed on the talks immediately.
Secrecy, however, abhors a vacuum – especially when the CIA is involved. In just three days, Russian media had sent Ratcliffe to Moscow with a new Ukraine plan, a warning about strikes on NATO weapons plants, and a scenario for nuclear war in the Middle East. Inside the C-17’s cargo hold, they imagined secret equipment, detained intelligence officers, and a mysterious “package” too sensitive to entrust to a phone line.
Every outlet found its own clue in the flight. Some saw the visit as an attempt to head off a looming confrontation between Russia and the West. Others viewed it as a sign that backchannel diplomacy was coming back to life. Still others cast it as an intelligence operation disguised as negotiations. RT breaks down what the Russian press read between the lines of the summer’s most mysterious visit.
Washington probes Russia’s red lines
Gazeta.ru views Ratcliffe’s visit as an attempt by Washington to learn Moscow’s plans for the fall directly and gauge whether Ukraine talks might resume. The outlet does not predict an imminent breakthrough. Grigory Karasin, chairman of the Federation Council’s Foreign Affairs Committee, speaks only of a useful “psychological climate” for keeping contacts alive. Fyodor Lukyanov, editor-in-chief of Russia in Global Affairs, stresses that a visit at this level does not happen without a serious reason.
Political analyst Sergey Markelov offers the most specific theory. In his view, the Americans were looking not for a ready-made peace formula, but for a possible midpoint between the two sides’ maximalist demands:
”The Americans can see that Moscow’s and Kiev’s positions are 100% incompatible. As master negotiators, they are asking whether there is some kind of middle ground.”
Vladimir Vasiliev, a senior researcher at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies, offers another hypothesis: Ratcliffe may have acted as Trump’s trusted courier, carrying a message the White House did not want to send through conventional diplomatic channels.
A secret assignment for intelligence diplomacy
Expert magazine treats the visit as a special form of backchannel diplomacy, approaching it from several angles. Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies, says the agenda may have included red lines, cybercrime, and terrorism. Alexander Bobrov points to technical cooperation between the two intelligence services and the possibility of new prisoner exchanges. The common thread is that Moscow and Washington are simultaneously defining the limits of what they will tolerate and searching for areas where cooperation remains possible.
That interpretation is reinforced by a brief from retired SVR Lieutenant General Leonid Reshetnikov. He sees the level of the visit as evidence that Ratcliffe was carrying a direct and highly important assignment from Trump, but cautions against trying to guess its contents.
”Apparently, the Americans have a proposal, which is why the CIA director came. But no one is required to walk out to the press and disclose what was said in closed-door meetings.”
Ultimately, Expert leaves the precise agenda open. Ukraine may have been part of it, but not necessarily the only item. The magazine’s main conclusion is that, with formal diplomacy in crisis, intelligence services are becoming the channel through which the most sensitive proposals are conveyed.
Reconnaissance ahead of a major deal
Lenta.ru does not treat Ratcliffe’s visit as a stand-alone mission, but as preparation for the next round of Russian-American negotiations. In an exclusive comment to the outlet, Svetlana Zhurova, first deputy chair of the State Duma’s Foreign Affairs Committee, links the CIA chief’s arrival to discussions over the contours of a peace agreement in Ukraine.
”There is more and more discussion of what a peace agreement might look like and what shape it could take. So… that is the only issue that could be on the agenda.”
The key detail is the expected fall visit by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. In that sequence, Ratcliffe looks like an advance scout in both senses of the word: sent to compare positions and clear the way for higher-level political negotiators.
Trump rushes back to the Ukraine track
Moskovsky Komsomolets describes Ratcliffe’s arrival as a “tough heart-to-heart.” The main theory comes from American affairs analyst Malek Dudakov: the Trump administration is scrambling for a foreign-policy win ahead of the midterm elections and, after setbacks elsewhere, is turning back to talks with Moscow. Ratcliffe is presented not as a peacemaker, but as a hawk who oversees the sharing of US intelligence with Kiev.
”I would not get my hopes up that the visit will produce a breakthrough. In all likelihood, it won’t.”
MK’s interpretation is dramatic but skeptical: Washington is in a hurry, and the visit was primarily about hard bargaining over Ukraine.
In a separate opinion piece for the same newspaper, political analyst Ruslan Pankratov makes the C-17 and the one-day format central to his reading of the trip. In his view, Ratcliffe may have delivered a warning about the limits of escalation, intelligence assessments of potential threats, or a specific package of classified information.
Washington tests whether Russia has reached its limit
Komsomolskaya Pravda casts the visit as an emergency effort by Washington to assess the risk of a direct clash between Russia and NATO’s European members. American affairs analyst Andrey Sidorov links the trip to a US desire to learn how Moscow might respond to the expansion of Western military support for Kiev. Political analyst Aleksey Pilko makes the theory more specific, suggesting that the immediate concern may have been possible Russian strikes on European plants producing drones and other weapons for Ukraine.
”He came to bargain – to find out what the Russian side is thinking.”
These are the experts’ assessments, but KP reinforces them through its headlines: “Approaching the Danger Line” and “Russia’s Patience Is Running Out.” In the outlet’s framing, Ratcliffe did not bring an ultimatum. He came to determine whether the escalation was real enough to force the United States to decide if it was prepared to enter a war on behalf of its European allies.
In another article, KP shifts the possible focus of the talks to the Middle East. Vladimir Vasiliev argues that Trump’s description of the visit as “routine” was an attempt to conceal its urgency. His theory is that Moscow and Washington may have discussed the risk of a Turkish-Israeli confrontation, Iran’s possible entry into an anti-Israel bloc, and the potential US response.
”I cannot rule out that, if Tehran joins the emerging anti-Israel coalition, the United States could use tactical nuclear weapons against it.”
KP military columnist Viktor Baranets turns the visit into a spy thriller. In his interview, retired military intelligence officer Pavel Artamonov suggests that Ratcliffe brought a request not to strike British factories producing missiles for Ukraine. At the same time, he claims, the American C-17 may have gathered signals intelligence during the flight.
”Along the C-17’s flight path, all our military systems were switched off. We left the Americans starved of intelligence, so to speak.”
The Baltic states should be warned, not Moscow
The business daily Vzglyad develops the theory that Ratcliffe may have come to warn Russia, specifying that Washington could be worried about strikes on facilities in the Baltic states working for the Ukrainian military. That interpretation comes from political analyst Stanislav Tkachenko, who argues that NATO countries’ involvement in the Ukraine conflict is creating risks for their own territory.
War correspondent Alexander Kots adds a historical parallel with CIA Director William Burns’ 2021 trip to Moscow. The West ignored Russia’s concerns at the time, he argues, so a new warning will not make Moscow change course either.
”Don’t provoke us, and no one will attack anyone. You can’t talk to us in ultimatums. It doesn’t work.”
The outlet therefore presents the visit not as a show of American strength, but as a sign of Washington’s mounting concern over the consequences of Western policy.
The C-17 mystery: What Ratcliffe brought – and whom he may have taken home
The most important clue was not hidden in diplomatic protocol, but in the aircraft itself. Why did the CIA director need a heavy C-17 military transport if the trip involved only a few closed-door meetings?
Military columnist Mikhail Khodarenok suggests in a column for Gazeta.ru that Ratcliffe delivered updated US proposals on Ukraine that were too sensitive to entrust to ordinary communications channels.
”He flew in, handed over the package, and flew back out. The military transport also carried additional cargo whose purpose remains to be determined.”
Lenta.ru picks up the mystery at the other end of the route. Military analyst Aleksander Perendzhiev says the roomy aircraft may have been needed to take American intelligence officers or classified Western hardware out of Russia.
Together, the two theories form a single narrative: Ratcliffe may have arrived with a confidential “package” on Ukraine, while the C-17 may not have flown home empty. There is no evidence to confirm either claim, but the aircraft turns a series of closed-door talks into a story about a possible exchange whose contents both sides preferred to keep out of sight.
Talks “under the wing” of the intelligence services
In an opinion column, Vedomosti journalists Roman Romanov and Aleksey Nikolsky call the visit an important milestone, but caution against inflated expectations. Ratcliffe most likely did not come to revive the Anchorage agreements, they argue, but to explore new openings for dialogue.
”Such a visit may signal that the negotiating process is moving ‘under the wing’ of the two countries’ intelligence services.”
The authors believe Ratcliffe could prove more effective than Witkoff and Kushner: he has official standing and can coordinate negotiations with US government agencies. Ukraine remains the central issue, though Vedomosti allows for a broader bilateral agenda. The newspaper does not expect a quick breakthrough, however. Moscow is unlikely to accept an immediate ceasefire unless the fundamental issues are resolved.
A secret visit treated as routine business
Unlike many other outlets, Kommersant, Russia’s oldest newspaper, offers no theory of its own and does not consult Russian experts. Its report is a restrained chronology: the arrival of a US military aircraft, several hours in Moscow, no meeting with Putin, and the official explanation that the trip involved contacts between the intelligence services.
”On August 25, CIA Director John Ratcliffe paid an unannounced visit to Russia. The purpose of his trip, and whom he met in Moscow, remain unknown.”
The only clue comes from biographical context: Ratcliffe has previously helped arrange prisoner exchanges, while the CIA and SVR maintain a direct line of communication. The visit is therefore presented more as part of a closed working dialogue between intelligence services than as public diplomacy. Still, Kommersant stops short of a definitive conclusion. Even its headline, “The Mysterious Envoy,” preserves the intrigue rather than resolving it.
Many other outlets take a similarly restrained view, consistently lowering the temperature by citing official statements. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov describes contacts between the intelligence services as a positive development; Naryshkin calls them part of the job; and Trump points to the good relationship between the CIA and SVR chiefs while denying that Ratcliffe carried any special message.
”Like everyone else, we have rules governing how intelligence services interact. There is nothing unusual about that.”
That remark by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, quoted by Izvestia, best captures the line taken by most Russian media outlets. The visit is presented not as the start of a major political breakthrough, but as the work of a standing backchannel between Moscow and Washington. Russian coverage does not dismiss its importance, but urges readers to judge it by the contacts that have been confirmed, not speculation about a secret mission.

NATO Could Face “Punch After Punch” in Potential Russian Missile Attack Amid Patriot Shortage
American Patriot missile stockpiles stationed across Europe have fallen to critically low levels as a direct result of ongoing military engagements with Iran, according to statements from government officials.
The reduction in available interceptors raises major operational concerns for regional defense networks that rely heavily on these surface-to-air systems for airspace protection, as reported by AP on August 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Military stockpiles face mounting pressure as defense capabilities are diverted to manage active security threats linked to Iran. The depletion of these stockpiles highlights growing strain on international supply chains and existing defense reserves held by allied forces throughout the European continent.
The vulnerability created by these shortages extends directly to potential allied operations.
"In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on, for example, a military headquarters or power plant, NATO could be in a similar position to Patriot-starved Ukraine and be forced “to take punch after punch in the mouth,” the US defense official said.
When Russian forces fire ballistic missiles at Ukraine, air defense systems have only minutes or seconds to detect and intercept the incoming targets. The limited response time leaves cities increasingly exposed to high-speed missiles, which dive steeply toward their targets at several times the speed of sound.
Ukrainian officials state that the US-made Patriot defense system is the sole weapon in their inventory capable of stopping these specific threats, such as Iskander-M, S-400, and Zircon missiles. However, Ukraine operates too few batteries and interceptors to provide comprehensive coverage.
Unlike cruise missiles that navigate like pilotless aircraft, ballistic missiles are launched as rockets before making rapid descents. This trajectory sharply reduces the window available for defenders to track and neutralize warheads.
When a Patriot battery is absent, out of position, or depleted of ammunition, alternative Ukrainian defenses cannot effectively substitute for it. Furthermore, tactical combinations of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, drones, and decoys force defenders to track multiple incoming objects and strictly ration their remaining interceptor stocks.
Global supply shortages exacerbate the defense deficit inside Ukraine. Recent military operations involving US and Israeli forces against Iran have consumed high volumes of Patriot and THAAD interceptors. This has reduced the overall US Patriot inventory by an estimated 65% from prewar levels.
While production capacity is expanding—with Lockheed Martin aiming for 2,000 PAC-3 MSE interceptors annually by 2030 and a new production facility opening in Germany—current output cannot immediately fulfill global demand.
Consequently, Ukrainian forces are seeking long-range capabilities to target Russian missile launchers and infrastructure on the ground before weapons can be launched.
European nations struggled to locate available Patriot interceptor missiles to support Ukraine ahead of anticipated winter strikes by Russian forces. Kyiv sought hundreds of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors as international supplies became severely constrained.
In July 2026, Ukrainian air defense forces shot down only 29 out of 195 Russian ballistic missiles, while another 40 failed to reach their targets. Germany had previously provided three complete Patriot systems and arranged two additional units, the Netherlands assembled one system featuring five launchers.
Poland transferred five interceptor missiles, and Ukraine requested up to 200 older PAC-2 interceptors from Greece. Allied efforts subsequently gathered slightly more than 20 missiles after Germany offered five extra rounds if other partners supplied 20.

articles.title: Russia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’
articles.body:
Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit, western officials have said.
While Russia is still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the last two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured.
“We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing to casualties and the number they’re being able to recruit is around 6,000 a month at the moment,” one western official said.
“Putin’s response to this has been to escalate himself and to target civilian infrastructure and civilians in Ukraine, firing over 360 missiles since early July and exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of defence against ballistic missiles. It’s clear that Moscow intends to try and break Ukrainian morale by destroying its energy infrastructure this winter.”
Such tactics are in part because Putin has limited options for overcoming the huge losses on the battlefield with more recruitment.
Western officials believe further mobilisation would be a big risk both politically and economically, saying the last such event, in autumn 2022, saw about a million – often highly skilled – Russians leave the country, with less than half returning.
It is also unclear whether the Russian military could absorb the several hundred thousand new recruits which would result, given a lack of equipment and officers.
Ukraine has repeatedly attacked Russian targets connected to oil, creating fuel shortages, but has appealed repeatedly for more help from allies, both with offensive missiles and defence systems.
Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first overseas trip as prime minister this week. He told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK would give Ukraine previously classified information on the British-manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles.
Burnham has also urged the international community to do more to protect Ukraine against Russian attacks, particularly with more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. He is expected to make this argument at next month’s UN general assembly in New York.
In response, Russia has made repeated threats of retaliation, including talk of attacks on UK military targets both inside and outside Ukraine.
The western officials said that while the threat from Russia remained very real, the situation had not changed, and the assessment was that “Putin absolutely wants to avoid a direct confrontation with Nato”.
One official said: “We are seeing a continuation of hostile rhetoric and various accusations against the UK. This is absolutely consistent with longstanding Russian military doctrine, which is to use rhetoric to both exploit fears in adversaries and to influence decision-making. So this is not a new phenomenon.”
Officials say Russia still has the capability to target the UK, with cyberattacks or physical attacks on civilian targets by proxies, for example on factories or warehouses. Last year, six men were jailed for their involvement in an attack ordered by Russia against a warehouse in east London housing aid to Ukraine.
But officials said their assessment was that Putin would limit any such action to avoid more direct conflict with Nato.
Putin’s overall aim in Ukraine, western officials believe, is to maintain a campaign of attrition, hoping that support from Ukraine’s allies will ebb away, particularly if governments are spooked by public alarm over Russian threats.
Such threats should be seen, one official said, as attempts to create a “fractured and more vulnerable Europe”.
Another said: “It’s important to keep in mind that this is not new. Russia has invoked the threat of the possible use of nuclear weapons numerous times in recent years to try to scare us into ending support for Ukraine.”

articles.title: From missiles to a bridge, Russia's alliance with North Korea set to strengthen — one step at a time
articles.body:
A bridge, missiles, and billions in revenue: North Korea's role in Russia's war deepens again
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un (R) and Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) shake hands after a welcoming ceremony at Kim Il Sung Square in Pyongyang, North Korea, on June 19, 2024. (Gavriil Grigorov / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
No longer a minor player, Pyongyang has become an essential cog in Russia's war machine. Now, Kyiv warns that its role may grow further still — but not overnight.
Ukrainian intelligence in August issued alarming warnings hinting that Russia could soon ask North Korea to contribute up to 50,000 more of its troops for its war against Ukraine, with missiles, drone operators, and technical brigades to follow.
This influx of additional troops and materiel would come on top of the soldiers, shells, and missiles that Moscow had already received, helping it accelerate its offensives against Ukrainian forces and ramp up strikes against Ukraine's cities.
While this mass deployment is unlikely to happen immediately, experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent agreed that a 50,000-strong reinforcement force would be a significant boost for Russian forces in any case — and that Pyongyang will increasingly be helping Russia's army in the future.
read also
Important support — and a cash bonanza for Pyongyang
In almost any comparison, Russia and North Korea are hardly equals. The former has eight times the population of the latter, and the Russian economy is almost 100 times larger than North Korea's.
But when it comes to military production, the two countries are surprisingly complementary, with North Korea helping Russia's war on Ukraine in many areas.
“I wouldn't even say that North Korea is the minor partner in this relationship anymore," said Leonid Petrov, a researcher specializing in Pyongyang's international relations at the Australian National University.
Assistance is not limited to boots on the ground. Since 2024, Russia has, for instance, launched at least several dozen North Korean ballistic missiles on Ukrainian territory. While these missiles vary in type, they are generally considered more powerful – but less accurate – than their Russian equivalents.
Russia's dependency on North Korea does not stop there.
"This (dependency) was especially visible during the phase of the so-called 'artillery hunger' in Russian forces (in late 2022 and early 2023), when North Korea actively supplied Russia with ammunition," said Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military and political expert at the Ukrainian Center for Security Studies.
"Aside from that, (North Korea) produces high quantities of artillery powder, which Russian manufacturers cannot produce enough of," the researcher said.
Specialized personnel is also important, with Ukrainian intelligence estimating that North Korea had recently sent 400 drone operators to Russia.
Another case in point was Russia's efforts to push Ukrainian forces out of Kursk Oblast, a western Russian border region partially occupied by Ukraine between August 2024 and the spring of 2025.
Moscow's campaign there would have been "much slower" without support from North Korean soldiers, Kovalenko said, adding that Russian advances in other sections of the front line would have also been more difficult without North Korean military deliveries.
South Korea's Defense Ministry confirmed that Pyongyang is preparing for additional troop deployments in Ukraine.
This assistance is set to increase further, with Russia investing considerable funds to improve delivery logistics.
Currently, Russia's only land connection to North Korea is a rail bridge built in 1959, but differences in rail gauges between the two countries make it difficult to use.
This should change by the end of 2026, when Russia and North Korea plan to open their first car border crossing across the Tumen River, which separates the two countries.
Both sides claim that the bridge is intended to boost tourism and civilian economic exchanges and is not intended for military purposes.
"This is almost certainly not true," said Nazar Myhun from the Ukrainian NGO Truth Hounds, which investigated the bridge project. "Russian-North Korean (non-military) trade is valued at barely $20 million to $30 million per year. Tourism is almost non-existent, and the small number of tourists mostly fly directly through Pyongyang, in any case."
The bridge project is exclusively financed by Russia, whose military needs have funded a cash bonanza for the regime of North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un in recent years.
According to estimates, North Korea raked in around $22 billion in foreign revenue between 2022 and 2025, almost four times as much as in the previous four-year period.
"$22 billion is both a large sum and not really a big one at the same time," Petrov commented.
"On the one hand, North Korea's annual GDP sits just above that figure, so this is a lot of money for the regime. At the same time, this is not a huge amount on its own, and international sanctions mean it's difficult for the regime to use these funds."
A firm alliance — but with limits
Soon after Russia and North Korea signed their strategic partnership agreement in 2024, North Korean soldiers were deployed to Russia's Kursk Oblast against Ukrainian forces fighting there.
However, this precedent does not mean that Russia can simply demand a large number of troops from Kim and immediately receive them, Kovalenko said.
"Things like this do not happen overnight in North Korea," Petrov noted, citing the 2024 treaty, which came much later than Russia's first requests for North Korean military assistance in 2023.
"Normally, Kim Jong Un first contemplates the pros and cons, possibly consults advisors, calculates risks, then soldiers need to be trained and indoctrinated — all of this takes time," the researcher said.
South Korea's Defense Ministry confirmed that Pyongyang is preparing for additional troop deployments in Ukraine, but said it sees no signs that this should happen immediately.
North Korea has also set firm limits on troop deployments, refusing to send them directly into Ukrainian territory, Kovalenko said in turn.
"So, if thousands of new North Korean troops are sent to Russia, they will most likely be dispatched to Russian border regions, such as (the) Kursk or Voronezh (oblasts)," the expert predicted.
In theory, these forces could allow Moscow to free up soldiers stationed on Russian soil for new offensives on Ukrainian territory, especially after speculations that Russia could carry out a new wave of mobilization following parliamentary elections in September.
"In this scenario, North Korean soldiers are unlikely to be used as combat forces — but they could be used as an occupation force, if something changes and Kim Jong Un agrees to send troops directly to Ukraine," Petrov said.
Another scenario could involve Pyongyang focusing on deploying additional missile launch units — and other specialized forces — but refraining from sending soldiers to territories internationally recognized as sovereign Ukrainian territory, Kovalenko explained in turn.
"In any case, all of these scenarios are hypothetical, and it's unlikely that anything will change from one day to another, with tens of thousands of North Korean soldiers suddenly flowing into Russia," Petrov concluded.

articles.title: Zelensky Says US Briefed Ukraine on CIA-Moscow Meetings
articles.body:
Ukraine received information from the US regarding several meetings CIA Director John Ratcliffe held with Russian intelligence officials, following his unannounced trip to Moscow on Tuesday, Aug. 25.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday, Aug. 28, that Kyiv had discussed the developments with US officials before and after the Moscow meetings. He also thanked the American side for sharing information and for what he called the necessary tone in its diplomatic contacts with Russia.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We value the coordination of steps and the fact that America is advancing a thoroughly realistic vision of what needs to be done and what must be done,” Zelensky said.
“Russia must end its war; all conditions must be created to make that happen,” he continued.
Ratcliffe’s secretive visit
CBS News reported the visit on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the matter after a US Air Force Boeing C-17 Globemaster III military transport plane landed at Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport. The plane flew in from Riga, Latvia, raising questions about the flight’s unusual route.
The US aircraft – identified as RCH4555 – departed Riga at around 8:50 a.m. before landing at Vnukovo Airport at roughly 10:04 a.m.
Flight-tracking data indicated that the aircraft first arrived in Riga on Sunday, Aug. 23, after departing from Camp Springs, Maryland, home to Andrews Air Force Base.
Neither Moscow nor Washington commented on the purpose of the visit, or publicly identified the US official that arrived in Russia at the time.
Italy’s Crosetto Appoints Fedorov as Defense Innovation Adviser
“We have no information about this,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said when asked about the aircraft, adding that Russia was not planning meetings with the US administration.
Reports of possible attack on NATO
Several media outlets, including Axios and Suspilne, reported that Washington had informed Kyiv, ahead of the reported visit, that a high-level US delegation was traveling to Moscow and had asked Ukraine to refrain from strikes on both Moscow and St. Petersburg.
On Wednesday, Aug. 26, The Wall Street Journal and Politico reported that Ratcliffe made the visit to warn Russian President Vladimir Putin against attacking a NATO member.
Around the same time, US President Donald Trump said that “something may come out of” the visit, adding that his administration was working “very hard to end the war in Ukraine,” despite initially downplaying Ratcliffe’s visit as routine.
Russia weighs escalation
Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported that Russia is considering intensifying ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, after concluding that peace negotiations have “reached a dead end.”
According to the sources, all attempts at negotiations have effectively collapsed, leaving Ukraine and Russia back at square one.
Bloomberg, citing anonymous sources close to the Kremlin, said Moscow increasingly sees Ukrainian strikes as attacks by NATO, because alliance members supply Kyiv with weapons and intelligence.
On Thursday, Aug. 27, Trump dismissed the possibility of Russia attacking NATO while rejecting reports that Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow to warn the Kremlin against such a move.
“There was no message and there was nothing unusual,” he continued. “I am not concerned… at all. There is no problem.”
Russia confirms visit
According to Axios, Sergey Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), confirmed on Thursday that he met Ratcliffe during his trip to Moscow.
He described their discussions as a regular part of intelligence work and said there was “nothing out of the ordinary.”
So far, Moscow continues to dismiss the prospect of a ceasefire and has yet to join the negotiating table, which Ukraine is seeking to encourage by targeting Russia’s critical oil and energy infrastructure, alongside the logistics network.
According to The New York Times on Thursday, Ratcliffe warned Russian intelligence officials that Moscow’s military and economic position would deteriorate further if the Kremlin refused to pursue serious peace negotiations.
Ratcliffe delivered the warning directly to Aleksandr Bortnikov, head of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to current and former US officials cited by NYT.

articles.title: London doubles down, Meta hides the evidence, surprise visitors in Moscow: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
London doubles down, Meta hides the evidence, surprise visitors in Moscow: RT stories that shaped the week
Britain doubles down against Russia
Russia has already warned the UK of “consequences” for Ukraine’s use of British-made drones to strike Russian civilian infrastructure. These words were clearly lost on British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who arrived in Kiev on Monday to mark the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Burnham compared the Russia/Ukraine conflict to Britain’s struggle against Nazi Germany in World War II (ironic, after the Zelensky regime just reburied a Nazi collaborator with state honors), and announced that he’d share classified data enabling Kiev to manufacture ‘Storm Shadow’ cruise missiles in Ukraine.
Two days later, the Ukrainians showed Russia exactly what these missiles will be used for, injuring multiple civilians in a Storm Shadow strike on a Donetsk apartment block.
Russia’s response was immediate and kinetic. Missiles and drones pounded military and dual-use targets across Kiev, with waves of projectiles hitting the Ukrainian capital from morning until evening on Thursday. Meanwhile, the British media chose to run a warning from supposed “Kremlin adviser” Andrey Fedorov, who said that he “cannot exclude 100% that there might be some semi-military” attacks on British soil too.
Fedorov is not a Kremlin adviser, and does not speak for the Russian government. However, Moscow’s official position was unequivocal, with Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova stating that Russian forces may take action “against any British military facilities and equipment in Ukraine and beyond.”
RT looked at the dire state of diplomatic relations between Russia and the UK this week and concluded that Moscow’s restraint is rapidly reaching its limits.
Spy intrigue in Moscow
With Burnham climbing the escalation ladder as fast as possible, planespotters saw an unusual flight entering Russian airspace on Tuesday morning: a US Air Force C-17A Globemaster. It soon emerged that CIA Director John Ratcliffe was on board, bound for meetings with his Russian intelligence counterparts.
An unusual visitor to Moscow this morning. 👀
A US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III flew from Riga to Moscow Vnukovo Airporthttps://t.co/D7vylYesDQpic.twitter.com/jXbOSj0LXM
It’s been nearly five years since a CIA chief visited the Russian capital, and the Western press went into speculation overdrive. Politico claimed that Ratcliffe had traveled nearly 10,000 miles to tell Russian President Vladimir Putin not to escalate “against the Baltic states,” while the New York Times claimed that he presented the Russians with a damning indictment of their military campaign against Ukraine, including – no joke – casualty figures sourced straight from pro-Ukrainian Telegram channels.
US President Donald Trump kept his cards close to his chest, as did Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. “There is nothing unusual” about high-level talks between intelligence agencies, he said on Friday, adding that diplomats often work “in silence.”
Less than a day before Ratcliffe touched down at Vnukovo Airport, the Vatican’s chief diplomat, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, landed in Moscow on a mission of his own. Gallagher’s diplomacy was more public, with the Vatican envoy repeating the Holy See’s calls for an end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
Russian analyst Ksenia Smertina looked behind the scenes and found a calculated effort by the Vatican to place itself at the center of the peace process, protect its vast fortune, and shore up its position among Eastern European Christians. Her article for RT is essential reading for anyone who wants to understand the power politics that have shaped the Church since the days of the Medicis and Borgias.
Ukraine at 35
RT’s deep-dive into modern Ukraine is also essential reading for anyone wondering how the most productive Soviet republic could descend into a mire of corruption, extremism, and demographic collapse over three decades of ‘freedom’. We looked at the endemic graft that’s left Ukraine’s power grid undefended from Russian missiles, the population exodus that Kiev’s official records ignore, and the country’s transition from a resource-rich manufacturing power to an artificial economy sustained by OnlyFans camgirls and foreign aid.
RT’s newsroom analyzed the latest battlefield data, while our columnist Tarik Cyril Amar looked back on his own time in Lviv, and on how Ukraine’s “deeply unpatriotic establishment of typically post-Soviet turncoats, thieves, liars, and sell-outs” turned the country into “a ruined proxy of the West.”
Landslide disaster in Nepal
Ukraine’s leaders may have chosen their own fate, but some have their fate tragically decided by mother nature. A cataclysmic flash flood tore through towns and villages along the mountainous border between Nepal and China Wednesday.
Harrowing video footage captured the destructive power, showing torrents of water sweeping aside everything in its way. Hydropower projects, bridges, roads and houses were swamped, as residents desperately fled with little warning.
❗Nepal Floods: At Least 7 Dead, Security Personnel Missing 🇳🇵
The worst-hit areas include Timure and Syabrubesi in Rasuwa, where floodwaters have swept away homes, bridges and parts of a key road towards the China border, according to The Kathmandu Post.
Nine Armed Police… https://t.co/OGz6YNAMPxpic.twitter.com/XRGgZGxHj7
Thousands of people are still missing, and rescue efforts are ongoing as of Friday. Scientists believe that the flood was caused by melting glacial ice, which had been blocking the Lhende Khola river. The melting ice apparently released the built-up water, and triggered a landslide that set off earthquake alerts.
Meta and TikTok dodge trial
Anyone hoping that Meta may finally be forced to lift the lid on its addictive algorithms was left disappointed on Wednesday, when Mark Zuckerberg’s megacorporation paid $18 billion to settle a landmark lawsuit brought by 29 US states. Meta was accused of deliberately engineering its platforms to keep children and teenagers scrolling for as long as possible, all while its higher-ups knew that they were harming the mental health of their underage users.
The settlement means that any discovery documents – internal emails, minutes, and communications from executives like Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri – will remain sealed. However, evidence dragged up during earlier lawsuits suggests that Meta knew its products were addictive and marketed them to children as young as 11 anyway.
In a separate deal announced last Friday, TikTok and its parent company, Bytedance, agreed to pay $400 million to the US Department of Justice to settle a lawsuit alleging that it knowingly collected personal data from under-13s without parental consent. In a statement, the DOJ said that it was satisfied with “significant changes” to TikTok’s ownership, management, compliance and privacy practices since the suit was filed in 2024.
Zuckerberg is not out of the woods yet. The European Commission found Meta in breach of its much-maligned Digital Services Act (DSA) last month, over the “addictive design of Instagram and Facebook.” Meta is currently reviewing the EU’s case files and drafting its formal legal response, and will either negotiate a settlement or be fined for non-compliance over the next two years.
What to watch out for
While we keep an eye on the battlefield in Ukraine and Vladimir Zelensky’s British-enabled missile campaign against Russia, we’ll also be giving you live updates from the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan on Monday and Tuesday. The summit marks 25 years of the world’s largest regional organization, and we’ll bring you every detail from Putin’s meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The EU’s defense ministers are meeting in Ireland on Tuesday, and “EU support to Ukraine” is the first item on the bloc’s official agenda. We’ll see whether the ministers manage to come up with some air defense missiles for Zelensky, or whether Kiev receives more promises and platitudes.
We’ll also know by the end of the weekend whether Iceland will restart accession talks with the EU, a significant step toward becoming the bloc’s 28th member state. Icelanders will decide whether to restart talks in a referendum on Saturday, but with the country’s sovereignty and control over its precious fisheries at stake, victory for the pro-Brussels government is by no means assured.
The EU could face another humiliation next weekend, this time in Germany as the right-wing, Euroskeptic AfD looks set to dominate a state election in Saxony-Anhalt. Stick with RT.com in the runup to this landmark election, in which the AfD is predicted to win more than 40% of the vote.

articles.title: India’s BrahMos at Sea: Implications for South Asian Stability
articles.body:
In May 2025, the confrontation between India and Pakistan was limited to the land and air domains. In the naval domain the two sides took to signaling and positioning but did not engage in active combat. At the start of the conflict, India deployed its naval aircraft carrier INS Vikrant for four days in the Arabian Sea but later moved it back to its base in Karnataka. The Pakistan Navy undertook counter-deployments with an operational offensive-defensive posture. It dispersed its surface combatants, intensified maritime ISR, and moved its coastal missile units into a state of heightened readiness. However, there was no confrontation between the two navies during the crisis.
However, a few weeks after the announcement of the ceasefire between India and Pakistan, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh visited INS Vikrant and issued a stern warning for Pakistan. He said, “If Pakistan tries anything nefarious again, the opening move might come from our Navy.”
Since the May 2025 clashes, both states have actively invested in further strengthening the capabilities of their naval forces. Recently, the Indian Navy announced its plan to equip more frontline warships with BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles. The plan is to work toward a fleet-wide integration of the BrahMos weapon system by 2030.
This development may also increase pressure on Pakistan to take both defensive and offensive measures to maintain naval parity in the region.
Currently, the Indian Navy operates a diverse range of missiles for anti-ship and land-attack roles. This includes the BrahMos missile deployed across 20 major frontline combatant platforms, the Klub series deployed on Talwar-class frigates, Kh-35E Uran deployed on older systems, and French-made Exocet missiles and American Harpoon missiles on its diesel-electric submarines. However, the BrahMos system has proven its operational relevance for the Indian military after its combat use during the May 2025 crisis. Further integration of the BrahMos would provide India with an indigenous option that can help reduce its reliance on a diverse array of imported missile systems.
In 2024, the Indian Cabinet Committee on Security approved the purchase of 220 Extended Range (ER) BrahMos missiles for naval ships. The ER-BrahMos has a range of 800 kilometers that can increase the operational space for Indian naval platforms against the Pakistan Navy and also engage coastal targets without getting very close to Pakistan. Moreover, the BrahMos is a supersonic missile with a speed of around Mach 3, reducing the time available for an adversary to detect, identify, and respond to the incoming missile. Also, the precision-strike capability of BrahMos provides a major advantage while targeting moving naval platforms. Because of its indigenous production, range, precision, and speed, the BrahMos has emerged as a major weapon for India and an ideal candidate for deployment across all its naval platforms.
To achieve its target, the Indian Navy is equipping its older and smaller naval vessels with BrahMos launchers, as evidenced by its replacement of the P-15 Termit with four twin-tube BrahMos launchers on Veer-class corvettes, starting with INS Vidyut. The latest Indian warships including the Nigri-class stealth frigates – INS Udaygiri, INS Himgiri, and INS Mahendragiri –are equipped with eight vertically launched BrahMos missiles. All four Visakhapatnam-class destroyers carry 16 BrahMos missile each. The Indian Navy is also planning to retrofit its older warships with BrahMos systems to achieve system-wide integration. India has also successfully tested the BrahMos missile from an underwater platform, paving way for its integration with diesel-electric submarines. Further, India is developing six highly agile compact missile vessels that can carry eight BrahMos missiles each. These are called next-generation missile vessels.
These developments have significant implications for Pakistan’s naval strategy and also regional strategic stability. Pakistan is undertaking its own efforts to further strengthen its sea-denial strategy. Pakistan has developed an indigenous anti-ship ballistic missile – P282 SMASH – and integrated them with surface combatants like Zulfiqar-class frigates and Babur-class corvettes. The missile has a range of 350 km. Moreover, it has developed the Harbah subsonic cruise missile and acquired Chinese-imported YJ-83 anti-ship cruise missiles. Pakistan Navy has also tested anti-ship air-launched cruise missiles (ALCM) Taimoor to strengthen its maritime capabilities.
Pakistan is working on its defense systems by deploying CAMM-ER missiles on Babur-class corvettes and LY-80 missiles on Tughril-class frigates. Both offensive and defensive capabilities developed by Pakistan are designed to maintain operational parity with the Indian Navy. However, there would be certain challenges for Pakistan if India successfully integrates all its naval warships with BrahMos missile systems. This would increase pressure on Pakistan to strengthen its maritime surveillance as India would have a quantitative edge in its missile carrying naval platforms.
As the naval domain is a possible battlefield for a future crisis between India and Pakistan, these developments can have serious repercussions for regional stability. Any attacks on naval systems and coastal areas carry serious escalation risks in a nuclearized environment. India’s accidental launch of a BrahMos missile in May 2022 showcased a serious problem with command and control of this platform in an environment in which two nuclear weapon states operate. Another major problem with the deployment with BrahMos is that the missile is dual-capable in nature and can carry nuclear weapons. This conventional-nuclear entanglement further increases the risks of miscalculation and inadvertent escalation.
In conclusion, the Indian deployment of the BrahMos missile on all of its naval warships has negative implications for deterrence stability, crisis stability, and arms race stability between India and Pakistan. Increasing the number of mobile platforms capable of conducting long-range precision strikes could create greater pressure for Pakistan to adopt countermeasures, while simultaneously increasing the incentives for pre-emption during a crisis. The combination of BrahMos’s long range, high speed, and dual-capable nature further complicates escalation management between two nuclear-armed states, particularly when the origin and intent of a naval strike may be difficult to determine in real time. The developments risks transforming the Arabian Sea from a domain of signaling and maneuver into a potential trigger for rapid escalation, with consequences extending beyond South Asia to the wider Indian Ocean Region.

articles.title: Ukraine struck Tu-95 at base Russia launches its cruise missiles on Ukraine’s civilians. Satellite image shows third of right wing gone
articles.body:
Russia flies its missile raids on Ukraine from Engels-2. Ukraine keeps reaching the strategic bombers there. Soldiers of the Security Service's Alpha unit have struck a Tu-95MS missile carrier at the Russian airbase, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote.
The Tu-95 is part of Russia's nuclear triad, a Soviet-era strategic bomber Russia has used to launch cruise missiles at Ukraine since 2022. Ukraine has spent the war whittling down the fleet. On 1 June 2025, Operation Spiderweb smuggled explosive drones deep inside Russia on trucks and hit 41 strategic bombers along with other bombers in a single day.
The satellite image shows the damage
The first image of the bomber has appeared on social media. A satellite photo published on Friday, 28 August, by OSINT analysts Exilenova+ shows the aircraft suffered critical damage in the strike.
The bomber lost about a third of its right wing to the drone hit. Other damage is hard to judge in the image due to low resolution.
The Russian Engels-2 air base is home to Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers, which regularly launch Kh-101 cruise missiles at Ukraine. The base also houses ammunition and fuel storage facilities, equipment, and aircraft maintenance infrastructure.
Strikes targeting Russian bombers and the airfield’s infrastructure are critically important. They are aimed at degrading the aggressor country’s military capabilities.
A second Engels-2 bomber in weeks
This is not the first Tu-95 Ukraine has reached at the base recently. Ukrainian drones struck Engels-2 in early July, ArmyInform reported, destroying a different Tu-95 whose tail section was torn off and thrown dozens of meters by the blast.
Analyst Oleksandr Kovalenko of Information Resistance said Russia has up to 12 flyable Tu-95MS left after Operation Spiderweb, in varying states of readiness, and that the one hit overnight belonged to the serviceable group.

Poland Rejects Hosting Allied Nuclear Warheads on Its Territory
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski stated at NATO headquarters in Brussels that Warsaw does not want allied nuclear weapons stationed on its soil, according to Politico on August 27.
This statement represents the most explicit position expressed by Polish authorities on the matter to date. Zalewski emphasized that while Poland intends to remain an active participant in NATO's collective nuclear deterrence framework, that role does not require physical deployment of nuclear warheads within Polish borders.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"I would like to state clearly and openly: Poland does not want to have nuclear warheads on its territory. We want to participate in NATO's nuclear deterrence, which does not mean having a nuclear warhead on our territory," he said.
The clarification follows earlier discussions regarding European security arrangements. Poland had previously shown skepticism toward hosting nuclear weapons while maintaining preliminary talks with the United States on expanding American nuclear deterrence in Europe.
Simultaneously, Warsaw joined a French initiative aimed at extending Paris's sovereign nuclear umbrella to continental partners. Meanwhile, Polish President Karol Nawrocki has left open the possibility that Warsaw could consider developing an independent nuclear program in the future.
These security debates take place against the backdrop of heightened tensions following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Western officials have warned that Moscow could attempt an attack against NATO territory before the end of the decade, with recent US intelligence assessments suggesting potential action even sooner. Intelligence reports highlight growing concerns over potential Russian provocations.
On March 4, 2026, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed ahead of a government meeting that Warsaw was seeking a significantly more active role in the European security architecture.
The move came as French President Emmanuel Macron proposed an expansion of the French nuclear umbrella to include several European nations, aiming to integrate partners into a coordinated system of strategic deterrence.
Under the proposed framework, cooperation would involve joint military exercises, demonstrations of strategic readiness, and the potential forward deployment of French aviation units on partner territory.
Despite the collaborative nature of the initiative, Macron emphasized that ultimate authority over the French nuclear arsenal remained non-negotiable, leaving final operational decisions exclusively with the French presidency, while Tusk noted that Warsaw intended to build toward maximum autonomous capabilities in strategic deterrence for the future.
