articles.title: A familiar business: Russia’s trade missions are replacing GRU spies with the friends and relatives of influential officials
articles.body:
Russian trade missions operate in more than 50 countries, and around a third of their staff are career military intelligence officers whose superiors do not work at the Ministry of Industry and Trade, but at GRU headquarters. The spies are tasked with assignments far removed from international commerce. According to a source, Minister of Industry and Trade Anton Alikhanov convinced Putin to replace half of the spies with actual subject-area professionals. But instead, the intelligence officers are simply being subbed out in favor of the relatives and friends of high-ranking officials.
The GRU’s warden for Austria
In August 2025, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, acting on a request from the Ministry of Industry and Trade, dismissed Russia’s trade representative in Austria, 67-year-old Andrei Plotnikov — purportedly due to “the expiration of his fixed-term service contract.”
Ever since the Soviet trade mission in Austria opened in 1921, the post of trade representative has always been reserved for a military intelligence officer. Outside the period of Nazi Germany’s occupation of Austria during WWII, Moscow’s representative in Vienna has always been a professional spy.
Trade representative Plotnikov worked in Austria for four years and gave interviews fairly often about trade turnover between the two countries. However, these conversations were merely cover. Plotnikov in fact held the rank of colonel and doubled as the deputy GRU station chief in Vienna, where he demonstrated solid operational results. Plotnikov’s espionage interests included local politicians and journalists, along with the heads of major firms. He also oversaw the Russian-Austrian Business Council, which stopped operating after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began.
“Andrei Nikolaevich [Plotnikov] was fired right after his birthday, and it was an undeserved insult. He’s a very well-known person, and they could easily have signed him to another three-year contract. Look at Alexander Bogatyr, who was in Cuba for nine years, and that was fine,” a source at the Ministry of Industry and Trade complained to The Insider.
At the GRU, Plotnikov was called “our legend,” and his superiors held him up as an example to other staff. When Plotnikov was still a young military intelligence officer, he was sent to West Berlin to serve as the Soviet warden at Spandau Prison. At the time, former close Hitler associate Rudolf Hess was still serving out his life sentence there. In 1987, Hess killed himself, and a version of the story still circulates among neo-Nazi groups that claim he was killed by British intelligence services. Plotnikov wrote a book, The Mystery of Rudolf Hess’s Death: A Warden’s Diary, in which he too arrived at highly questionable conclusions.
After Germany, Plotnikov continued his GRU service and graduated from the Military Diplomatic Academy. He was then assigned to Rosvooruzheniye (now Rosoboronexport, the Russian state-owned defense export agency), where he headed the Southeast Asia desk. From 2003 to 2009, Plotnikov spied in China under cover as a Russian trade mission employee, and before being sent to Austria, he headed Rostec’s representative office in Germany.
Following a series of high-profile spy scandals resulting from reporting by The Insider, Austrian authorities have begun paying much closer attention to Russian diplomats and journalists. The Austrian Foreign Ministry rejected all trade representative candidates proposed by Moscow, forcing the mission to draw on personnel already present in Vienna.
The initial candidate for “chief trader” was Alexander Zherikhov, whose father, Alexander Zherikhov Sr., headed Russia’s customs service from 2004 to 2006 and now holds the post of advisor to the CEO of Gazprom Neft. However, Artem Klimentyev was put in charge of trade instead.
Klimentyev’s mother, Svetlana, is a well-known figure in financial circles, previously working at Mezhprombank and at the Moscow representative office of the now-defunct British company Fort Trading Corporation Limited. Svetlana currently works on the management side of the Moscow Venture Fund.
Klimentyev himself graduated from the Academy of Foreign Trade, and in 2018 his mother arranged for him to become a consultant in the Department of European and North American Countries and International Organizations at the Ministry of Economic Development. From there, he moved to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, where he headed a department until his departure for Austria.
Notably, the reshuffle in Vienna did not help improve trade turnover between the two countries, which in 2025 was down by 74% year-on-year, with a further decline expected for 2026.
Algeria, the gateway to Africa
The dismissal lists at the Ministry of Industry and Trade are drawn up by First Deputy Minister Kirill Lysogorsky, who directly oversees the trade missions. As it turns out, Lysogorsky is far from an outsider to the GRU — a graduate of the Russian Military Academy of the Strategic Missile Forces, he previously headed government departments connected with the defense industry and arms supplies.
“Lysogorsky may be an important figure now, but he used to be just an errand boy running after Deputy Prime Minister Yuri Borisov — together they traveled to half the world,” a source at the ministry told The Insider.
In addition to Plotnikov, in September 2025 career GRU officer Ivan Nalich, Russia’s trade representative in Algeria, was put on Lysogorsky’s “chopping block.” Nalich had worked in North Africa for eight years and had built up an extensive network of contacts among military officers, officials, and public figures. “Algeria is the gateway to Africa,” Nalich said in one interview.
“Trade representative” Nalich also has a classic spy’s biography. In 2003, he graduated from the Institute of Asian and African Studies at Moscow State University, where he appears to have caught the eye of GRU recruiters. After graduation, Nalich took a job at the RIA Novosti state news agency, covering Middle Eastern affairs. In 2005, he moved to Rosoboronexport. Then, from 2009 to 2011, he worked in various positions at Rostec before returning to Rosoboronexport. Nalich subsequently spent five years spying in Morocco before being sent to Algeria as trade representative in 2019.
Nalich seems to have inherited a knack for espionage from his KGB grandfather.
The GRU now has a standing joke that after being fired from the Ministry of Industry and Trade, Nalich will become a backup dancer for his cousin — the well-known performer Pyotr Nalich.
In place of Nalich, Prime Minister Mishustin appointed 56-year-old Alexei Shatilov as Russia’s new trade representative in Algeria. Shatilov had worked for the Presidential Executive Office since the late 1990s in several capacities, and his last post at the Presidential Executive Office was as advisor in the foreign economic activity department of the president’s expert directorate. He had previously worked as trade representative in Algeria and had also spent time in the UAE and Qatar. He is considered to be part of the inner circle of Igor Neverov, head of the president’s foreign policy directorate. Neverov is said to have lobbied for his protégé’s reappointment to Africa.
In a recent interview, Shatilov praised Algeria for its pro-Moscow orientation and encouraged Russian companies to enter the local market. The trade representative did not mention, however, that the country is considered one of the most corrupt in Africa. The initial budget for the highway connecting Algeria with Morocco and Tunisia was $6 billion, but corruption drove the final cost to $17 billion — including $5 billion in kickbacks for local officials.
A comedian replaces a smuggler
In January 2023, Cuba welcomed a new Russian trade representative, Sergei Baldin. Before Havana, he had headed the trade and economic department at the Russian embassy in Portugal and the Russian trade mission in Brazil.
An analysis of Baldin’s activities shows that in Brazil he mainly represented Rosoboronexport’s interests. For example, the trade representative actively negotiated Russia’s entry into the Latin American arms market and took part in Latin America Aero & Defence military fairs in Rio de Janeiro.
Baldin is also credited with the successful negotiations to establish visa-free travel between Russia and Brazil, a development that clearly pleased the GRU and the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). While in Cuba, Baldin spoke in interviews about the good prospects for trade between Moscow and Havana. However, in June 2026, he unexpectedly resigned before his contract had even ended.
As The Insider learned, Baldin had concealed from his superiors at the Ministry of Industry and Trade the fact that he was being prosecuted for smuggling. On May 2, 2021, he flew into Moscow’s Sheremetyevo Airport from Lisbon and headed for the exit through the green channel. When a customs officer asked whether he had any undeclared currency, Baldin said no. However, during an inspection, officers found nearly $52,000 on him.
Trade representative Baldin concealed from his superiors at the Ministry of Industry and Trade the fact that he was being prosecuted for smuggling
To replace Baldin, Moscow appointed Vakhtang Mosashvili as its new trade representative. His father, Vyacheslav Mosashvili, is a close acquaintance and former Ministry of Transport colleague of Putin aide Igor Levitin.
The younger Mosashvili’s résumé, obtained by The Insider, matches all of the expectations for a member of a nomenklatura family: “Attended a school at the Russian embassy in Belgium, graduated from the law faculty of the Russian State University for the Humanities. Worked at Aeroflot and at trade missions in Hungary and Spain.”
In the Russian mission in Havana, Mosashvili is known as an irrepressible “jokester,” the life of the party at gatherings, and a fan of off-color jokes. The trade representative’s peculiar sense of humor is showcased in his now-deleted account on Odnoklassniki social network, where he wrote about himself: “Three years’ imprisonment under Article 162, Part 1 of the Russian Criminal Code, ‘Robbery,’ served at the PLS penal colony in Solikamsk. Broke, I don’t have a car, I curse, I’m schizophrenic, neurasthenic, asthmatic, I pick my nose, I have dandruff, worms, gonorrhea, I sniff glue, gasoline, and stain remover.”
A few more “trade representatives” from military intelligence also fell under Deputy Minister Lysogorsky’s cuts, but no replacements have yet been found for them. Vladislav Darvay left Moldova in September 2024, and The Insider later published wiretaps which showed that he had organized a visit to Russia by fraudster-oligarch Vladimir Plahotniuc, who stands accused of involvement in running $20 billion in corrupt Russian money through the “Moldovan laundromat”. Plahotniuc met with Kremlin official Dmitry Kozak and discussed interference in Moldova’s elections. However, the plan fell through when Plahotniuc was arrested, Kozak was fired, the Kremlin’s preferred candidates lost the election, and Darvay was barred from entering the country.
In Syria, espionage will continue
In some countries, however, Russian spies have not been replaced by “well-connected” substitutes from the civilian sector. In Syria, for instance, the GRU again managed to appoint one of its own to the trade representative post — 55-year-old career intelligence officer Vladimir Noskov. He replaces GRU officer Georgy Asatryan, who was recalled to Moscow and put forward for an award for the successful evacuation of Russian military personnel and equipment from bases in Syria to Libya.
Colonel Noskov graduated from the Military Diplomatic Academy, was seconded to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and spied in Lebanon, Egypt, and Qatar (facts that did not prevent his son from getting a job at Bain & Company, a U.S. entity closely tied to Anatoly Chubais).
As for his appointment to Syria, it is likely that no one from the “well-connected” crowd, accustomed to a comfortable life, wanted an assignment to that troubled country.

articles.title: Ukraine maps supply chain behind Russian Iskander missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military intelligence has published new data identifying components, companies and individuals it says are connected to production of Russia’s 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missile, including dozens of foreign-made electronic parts found in recovered weapons.
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence, known as the GUR, said in a statement published on Telegram that the latest release adds information on 140 Russian and foreign components, 35 enterprises and 108 officials and employees associated with the missile’s production chain.
The information has also been added to Ukraine’s War&Sanctions database, where the GUR is beginning a wider series examining Russian ballistic missile production and the industrial networks supporting it.
The combined database presented by Ukrainian intelligence is broader than the newly released material. According to the GUR, it now contains an interactive model of the 9M723 and information on more than 170 identified components, 82 Russian and two Belarusian companies involved in the production chain, 108 officials and employees, and 121 pieces of foreign-made manufacturing equipment used by the companies concerned.
Of the 140 components newly disclosed, Ukrainian intelligence said only around a quarter were manufactured by Russian companies. It attributed 63 components to US manufacturers, eight each to Switzerland and Belarus, four each to Germany and Taiwan, and three to China.
The GUR drew particular attention to electronics used in a flight-information processing unit associated with the missile’s laser gyroscope. According to the Ukrainian agency, five of 43 identified components in that unit were Russian-made.
Foreign components identified by the GUR include microprocessors, field-programmable gate arrays, memory devices and digital-to-analogue and analogue-to-digital converters. Manufacturers named by the agency include DM&P Electronics, Xilinx, now part of AMD, Atmel, now part of Microchip Technology, Winbond Electronics, Micron Technology and Analog Devices.
The presence of a commercially produced component inside a Russian weapon does not by itself establish that the manufacturer supplied the Russian defence industry directly. Electronic components can move through distributors, intermediaries and secondary markets before reaching their eventual end user, while Western governments have progressively tightened export controls intended to restrict Russian access to sensitive technology since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Ukrainian intelligence said the latest disclosure was intended to provide governments with additional information for sanctions and export-control measures targeting Russia’s ballistic missile supply chain.
The GUR also used the publication to make new claims about an updated version of the Iskander missile. It said Russian forces had employed an upgraded weapon designated 9M723-2 during a combined missile attack on Kyiv during the summer, describing the missile as also being known as “Iskander-1000” and associating it with a system called “Bora-M”.
According to the Ukrainian intelligence assessment, the modified missile uses a larger propulsion section and launcher and has a claimed range of up to 550 kilometres, compared with approximately 390 kilometres for the 9M723-1 configuration cited by the agency. The GUR said other elements of the missile remained largely identical to those of the earlier version.
Those details represent the Ukrainian intelligence service’s assessment of the recovered weapon and have been presented by the agency as part of its analysis of Russian ballistic missile development.
The 9M723 is the ballistic missile associated with Russia’s road-mobile Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system. Russia has used Iskander ballistic missiles extensively against targets in Ukraine, alongside air-launched missiles, cruise missiles and increasingly large numbers of uncrewed attack aircraft.
Image Vitaly V. Kuzmin.

articles.title: Iran may be the key to the Mecca Pact’s future
articles.body:
Iran may be the key to the Mecca Pact’s future
The reported invitation for Iran to join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement puts a new perspective on what the new alliance might ultimately become.
Mehdi Rahimi, head of the Iranian parliament’s news agency, said that the proposal was under consideration by the country’s leadership and argued that the creation of a regional security umbrella would represent a victory for the Islamic Republic. Shortly afterwards, however, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei stated that Tehran had received no formal invitation, although proposals for dialogue with the pact’s members on collective regional security had indeed been raised. For the moment, this appears to be a political overture intended to test the reactions of the parties rather than the beginning of a formal accession process. Even so, it suggests that the agreement is not intended as an alliance against Tehran, but as the possible foundation of a security system built with Iranian participation.
The Mecca Agreement was signed on August 7 by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Its central provision declares that an armed attack against one member will be regarded as an attack against all. The formula theoretically combines a formidable set of capabilities: Saudi Arabia’s immense financial resources and influence over global energy markets, Türkiye’s large military and sophisticated defence industry, and Pakistan’s substantial military experience and nuclear arsenal. Yet the public statements offer no detailed decision-making procedure and do not specify what action each signatory would be obliged to take during a crisis. At this stage, the pact is only a political declaration of collective deterrence and not a proper military alliance.
Erosion of the American monopoly
Donald Trump welcomed the pact and expressed satisfaction that the states of the region were finally assuming greater responsibility for their own defense. His response was consistent with his longstanding view that Washington’s allies should bear a larger share of military expenditure, allowing the US to reduce its costs and step back from the role of unconditional guarantor of other nations’ security. Seen from this perspective, the agreement might appear to be a success for American policy, since three US partners are establishing an additional mechanism of deterrence without Washington’s direct involvement.
Yet behind this public enthusiasm lies a trend that is far less favorable to the US. The Mecca Pact cannot be described as the first symptom of declining American influence in the Middle East, but it is the clearest institutional sign to date that regional powers no longer regard the American security umbrella as sufficient and have begun constructing autonomous centers of power. Washington retains its military bases, weapons systems, intelligence capabilities and relationships with regional elites, but it is gradually losing its monopoly over the rules by which Middle Eastern security is organized.
The US-Israeli war against Iran accelerated this transformation because it revealed the double-edged nature of American security guarantees. The US military presence may deter adversaries, but it can also draw the Gulf states into conflicts whose timing and objectives are determined without their meaningful participation. Iranian strikes, disruption to maritime trade and threats to energy infrastructure demonstrated that a close partnership with Washington does not insulate regional states from danger and may instead force them to bear the consequences of American policy.
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan are not abandoning American weapons or political ties, yet they want a mechanism capable of functioning even when Washington’s priorities diverge from their own.
Iran could transform the pact into a security system
For the pact’s three founding members, the possibility of inviting Iran addresses a problem that might otherwise have become the source of another major conflict. As long as Tehran remained outside the agreement, it could interpret the partnership between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan as an attempt to build a Sunni military bloc directed against the Islamic Republic.
By offering Tehran a place at the table, the pact’s founders have effectively replaced the question of whom the alliance is directed against with the question of which rules the region’s principal powers are prepared to accept. Even if Iran never joins, the dialogue itself reduces the likelihood that the agreement will automatically become an instrument of its isolation. Saudi Arabia gains an opportunity to combine military deterrence with continued diplomatic de-escalation, Türkiye strengthens its role as a mediator, and Pakistan avoids having to choose between its strategic partnership with Riyadh and its relationship with neighboring Iran.
Full Iranian participation could transform the nature of the pact itself. It would cease to be an alliance among states united by similar fears and would instead become a mechanism of mutual restraint in which one member’s security could not be achieved through another’s vulnerability. A declaration of collective defense alone, however, would not be enough. The participants would need emergency communication channels, rules for preventing military incidents, mechanisms for exchanging information on missile launches, guarantees of freedom of navigation and commitments not to support armed action against fellow members.
The most difficult issue would concern the non-state armed groups aligned with Iran. If Tehran joined the pact, it would inevitably be expected to assume political responsibility for the actions of forces receiving Iranian weapons and support. At the same time, the other members would have to refrain from exploiting Iran’s internal divisions as a means of exerting pressure on its leadership. Only such reciprocity could turn an appealing formula into a functioning regional order.
The economic prospects
Iran’s potential inclusion could initiate not only a political renaissance but also a major economic advance, since the development of the Middle East has been constrained for decades not by a lack of resources, but by chronic uncertainty. Wars raise shipping insurance costs, compel governments to accumulate weapons, discourage long-term investment and turn transport corridors into instruments of geopolitical bargaining. Even a partial reduction in these risks would release resources currently devoted to preparing for the next crisis.
Saudi capital, Turkish industry, the Pakistani market and Iran’s energy and transit potential could complement one another. Their cooperation could create new routes connecting Central Asia, the Persian Gulf, the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, while the security of the Strait of Hormuz could be transformed from an instrument of mutual coercion into a shared interest. A region long seen as mostly a theater of war and foreign intervention would gain an opportunity to become an autonomous economic center within an increasingly multipolar world.
The economic dividend, however, is not guaranteed. Continuing sanctions against Iran, competition over transport routes, clashing Turkish and Saudi ambitions, and Pakistan’s disputes with India could import old conflicts into the new arrangement. The pact’s success will depend on the ability of its members to separate collective security from temporary alignments and to prevent every bilateral confrontation from becoming an obligation for the entire coalition.
Israel’s choice
The most difficult external question concerns the future relationship between the Mecca Pact and Israel. Israel is already uneasy about the agreement, and would likely find the accession of Iran unacceptable, seeing it as the beginning of strategic encirclement.
Even with Iran, however, the pact does not have to become an alliance against Israel. If its members firmly establish the defensive nature of the agreement and offer Israel mechanisms for preventing conflict, it could restrain escalation rather than prepare the ground for it. The problem is that the current Israeli leadership has grown accustomed to pursuing security through the unrestricted use of unilateral force, whereas a regional system requires agreed rules and recognition that neighboring states also possess legitimate security interests.
Much will become clearer after the Knesset election scheduled for October 27, 2026. If Benjamin Netanyahu and the far-right bloc remain in power, tensions are likely to intensify, particularly if Israel continues its strikes against Iran and Syria while treating Türkiye’s growing influence as a direct threat. In that event, the Mecca Pact may evolve not simply as an alternative to weakening American guarantees, but as an instrument for deterring Israeli military action.
An opposition victory would not guarantee peace, since a hard line on Iran and national security extends far beyond Netanyahu’s political camp. Nevertheless, a new coalition might choose normalization over the endless expansion of conflict and attempt to incorporate Israel into the emerging regional balance.
The Mecca Agreement is not a new Middle East Order – merely a promise of one. Yet if it manages to accommodate Iran as a member, establish clear rules of mutual restraint and find a form of peaceful coexistence with Israel, the Middle East could for the first time in decades have a security system created primarily by the states of the region. Such a system would not eliminate their differences, but it could allow them to work with and around those differences without constant recourse to an external hegemon and without turning every crisis into a war. The cradle of the Abrahamic faiths might then cease to be consumed by recurring fires and begin its transformation into a strong, interconnected and prosperous region.

articles.title: Over 3 killed, more than 30 injured as Russia, Ukraine trade overnight strikes
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
At least three people were killed and more than 30 others injured as Russia and Ukraine traded overnight strikes, local authorities said Friday.
In Russia, Yaroslavl Governor Mikhail Yevrayev claimed on Telegram that 67 drones were downed over his region as Ukraine launched an overnight drone attack.
“One person was killed in the attack. Ten people were injured when debris fell on an inter-municipal bus. Another 17 people also sustained injuries of varying severity,” Yevrayev said.
Stating that drone debris fell on industrial infrastructure, residential areas, and retail facilities in the region, Yevrayev added that fires that occurred as a result of the attack were being quickly extinguished.
Andrey Vorobyov, governor of the Moscow region, said that a store belonging to food retailer Magnit in the town of Pavlovsky Posad was hit during a morning strike, which also damaged a nearby clinic.
Separately, Mikhail Razvozhayev, the Russian-installed governor of Sevastopol in Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014, said four people were injured following a drone strike on a five-story apartment building.
Ukraine’s General Staff claimed it struck the Yaroslavl refinery operated by Russian oil company Slavneft, causing a fire on the facility’s grounds. It said that the enterprise is involved in “supplying the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later claimed on US social media company X that his country's Security Service also struck a Tu-95MS aircraft in the city of Engels in Russia's Saratov region. Moscow has not commented on the claim.
The Russian Defense Ministry claimed that its air defenses downed 512 Ukrainian drones over 18 regions, as well as over the Black Sea and Crimea.
Strikes in Ukraine
In Ukraine, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv City Military Administration, said that one person was killed and two others were injured as Russian strikes targeted the region surrounding the capital.
“Under the attack of enemy drones are civilian objects: private and apartment buildings, warehouses, cars, and enterprises. Currently, 14 warehouses, 16 private households, three apartment buildings, 16 vehicles have been damaged in the region,” Tkachenko said.
Ukraine’s private postal and courier company Nova Poshta announced that its sorting centers in the Kyiv and Sumy regions came under attack overnight.
Sumy Governor Oleh Hryhorov said that one person was killed and seven others were injured following a strike by guided aerial bombs on the region’s administrative center.
Elsewhere, Zaporizhzhia Governor Ivan Fedorov said that four people were injured as a Russian drone hit a hypermarket belonging to Epicentr, a Ukrainian retail and construction chain.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defenses shot down 137 out of 164 drones launched by Russia overnight.
Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that it struck a warehouse complex in the Kyiv region “used to store finished products of Flamingo long-range cruise missiles and fuel for rocket boosters.”
The ministry also claimed that six storage facilities in the port of Odesa “containing military equipment intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces” were hit.
Independent verification of either side’s claims is difficult due to the ongoing war.

articles.title: Russia loses 6,000 more troops every month than it manages to recruit – The Guardian
articles.body:
Russia loses 6,000 more troops every month than it manages to recruit – The Guardian
Kyiv • UNN
Russia recruits around 30,000 troops every month but loses 6,000 more. A new mobilization threatens the Kremlin with political risks.
The Russian army’s monthly losses in Ukraine exceed the number of newly recruited personnel by approximately 6,000, and over the past two months recruitment has no longer compensated for the losses. The Guardian reports this, citing assessments by Western officials, writes UNN.
Details
Russia continues to recruit around 1,000 people into the military each day. However, according to assessments by Western officials, over the past two months this has proved insufficient to replenish its losses.
We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing as a result of combat and the number it is managing to recruit currently stands at around 6,000 people per month
The West believes that, amid a personnel shortage, Russia is intensifying strikes on Ukraine’s civilian and energy infrastructure. According to the publication, since the beginning of July, Russian forces have launched more than 360 missiles, in particular exploiting Ukraine’s shortage of means to counter ballistic missiles.
Mobilization remains a risk for the Kremlin
Western officials believe that a new wave of mobilization would create significant political and economic risks for Russia. After mobilization was announced in the autumn of 2022, around one million Russians left the country, many of them highly skilled professionals.
There is also the question of whether the Russian army will be able to receive, train and equip several hundred thousand recruits due to shortages of equipment and officers.
According to assessments by Western intelligence services, Putin seeks to continue a war of attrition against Ukraine, counting on the gradual weakening of allied support for Kyiv. At the same time, Western officials believe that the Kremlin is trying to avoid direct confrontation with NATO, while using threats against Europe to intensify divisions among European countries.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1647: Kyiv is under nonstop attack for a second day as Russia’s strikes wipe out 90% of Ukraine’s modern commercial storage
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Fix for Ukraine's interceptors is radar seeker head, and American firm is selling one for $4,000, says president's tech adviser. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov says cloud and fog collapse interceptor hit rates, and a seeker head is the way out.
Four ground robots for one evacuation: Russia is targeting Ukraine's robotic medevac missions. Ground robots are helping evacuate wounded troops from exposed positions, but the systems themselves have come under intense Russian fire.
Ukrainian robot commander calls ground robots "Persian elephants." What army really needs are "Arabian steeds", he says. A "Khartia" robot commander says FPV drones and mines have collapsed the machines' lifespan.
Ukraine has built twin-Kalashnikov turret for cheap ground robots. Security Service has already used one to destroy Russian ambushes. A Brave1 turret carries two AKs and went from idea to prototype in under six months.
Ukraine struck Tu-95 at base Russia launches its cruise missiles on Ukraine's civilians. Satellite image shows third of right wing gone. SBU Alpha struck the strategic bomber at Engels-2.
Kyiv has been under attack for 2 days nonstop. Russia is targeting the capital's civilian supply chains. Russian jet-powered drones have repeatedly struck warehouses, businesses and logistics facilities around the capital, disrupting supplies while rescuers work under threat of further attacks.
Intelligence and technology
Partisans say Russian recruiters in occupied Donetsk are taking drunk men from bars straight to enlistment offices. An ATESH agent inside the Dnepr grouping headquarters reports a new scheme.
Russians bought $300 million in body armor, thermal sights, and drone parts on Ozon marketplace Ukraine is bombing. Russians bought 157,700 body armor vests there.
Russia is secretly building a mortar-launched drone-killer—and a resistance group just leaked the blueprints. Leaked documents describe a swept-wing drone built to hunt other drones at up to 300 km/h. Russian firm NIK allegedly cooperated with Boeing.
International
Ukraine dismissed its defense minister in July. He is now advising NATO country on defense innovation. Guido Crozetto called the dismissed Ukrainian minister the day after Kyiv let him go.
From the Gripen sale to coast guard boats—Sweden sends 10 vessels to Ukraine. Ukraine's emergency service will use the boats for waterborne rescue work, including clearing mines from river beds. Stockholm's contributions to the US-led PURL program now total $552 million.
Poland kept selling itself as Kyiv's gateway to Europe—Ukraine stopped needing one, Polish journalist argues. Russian disinformation moved into the gap the two governments left, hardening a rupture neither of them prepared for, he wrote.
Sofia gets seven minehunters from Belgium and the Netherlands for a sea Russia mined. Parliament signed off on two separate agreements this week, one a purchase and one a transfer, with the Dutch side restoring part of the fleet before it changes hands.
Moldova is investing in air defense against the Russian drones crossing from Ukraine—Romania shoots down the ones that reach it. Allied fighters over the neighboring NATO member have destroyed intruding drones repeatedly this year, while the neutral country in between can track them crossing but not shoot them down.
A suspected Russian scheme to obtain Finnish citizenship ran for more than 20 years before Finland noticed. Police and the Border Guard say the size of what they uncovered took them by surprise, and that several naturalizations were still moving through the system when the inquiry opened.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russia destroyed last of Kherson's heat and power equipment on 26 August. Ukraine's new defense minister arrived days later. Yevhenii Khmara met the regional governor days after glide bombs wrecked the city's power plant.
Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine's modern commercial storage capacity. Retail logistics are being reshaped. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi says the country faces no threat of famine, but warns stores could see a narrower range of products.
Political and legal developments
“Territory that will allow us to export our energy resources to Europe”: Russia's deputy Duma chairman calls for massed bombing of Ukrainian cities. Duma vice-speaker Pyotr Tolstoy said the aim is to demoralize civilians until they give up.

articles.title: Russia is secretly building a mortar-launched drone-killer—and a resistance group just leaked the blueprints
articles.body:
A Russian drone company is developing an interceptor drone—the cheap counter-drone weapon Ukraine has fielded at scale against Russian attack drones—internal documents published by the Russian resistance group Black Spark describe, the defense outlet Militarnyi reported. The documents describe two designs under consideration, and Black Spark alleges the company cooperated with Boeing before the full-scale invasion and spied on European companies.
Interceptor drones—unmanned aircraft that hunt other drones—scaled up out of Ukraine's need to shoot down Russia's mass Shahed attacks without spending million-dollar missiles on them. Ukraine now fields them from dozens of licensed makers, and their spread has pushed Russia toward faster jet-powered attack drones. Russia already flies anti-drone interceptors of its own—Ukrainian troops downed one in July—and the leaked designs would fly far faster than that machine.
Mortar-launched drone-killer
NIK is considering two interceptor designs. The first modifies the company's existing UBB-M, a folding-wing loitering munition that launches from a 160 mm container by mortar-style ejection. For the interceptor role, designers changed the wing from straight to swept, shrank the wingspan, installed a larger battery, and fitted a more powerful motor.
The modified drone weighs 15-16 kg, carries a 3 kg payload—likely a warhead—and flies at 250-300 km/h with a 20 km operating radius and up to 10 minutes of flight time, operating between 20 meters and 4.5 km altitude. NIK's second design has a cone-shaped fuselage with four electric motors. Its specifications remain unknown.
Espionage claim comes with no documents
Black Spark says the documents came from someone inside the company, not a break-in, and that it holds evidence the firm spied on European companies. It gave no details on the Boeing cooperation beyond dating it before the invasion.
The leak is Black Spark's latest operation against Russia's defense industry. The group, which operates inside Russia, says it infiltrated the Alabuga factory where Russia assembles Shahed-derived Geran drones and copied personnel databases. Ukraine's Special Operations Forces have acknowledged joint missions with Black Spark, including attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.

articles.title: Berlin refutes media reports about talks on financing modernization of UK nuclear arms
articles.body:
BERLIN, August 28. /TASS/. The German government has denied The Daily Telegraph’s reports saying that Germany is allegedly in talks on potential financing of the United Kingdom’s nuclear weapons modernization program.
"We can refute what is reported there (in the newspaper - TASS). There are neither talks on financing nor any such plans," German government spokesman Steffen Meyer said. He recalled that Germany is negotiating closer cooperation on deterrence issues with France, but, in his words, this is about a "purely complementary nature" of cooperation within NATO on this matter.
The Daily Telegraph reported earlier, citing sources, that Germany is negotiating to serve as a financier in the United Kingdom’s nuclear weapons modernization program. According to the newspaper, Berlin is interested in establishing cooperation with London and Paris on a range of nuclear deterrence issues in light of the fact that the US President Donald Trump administration is no longer viewed as a reliable ally. As such, Germany wants to help the United Kingdom build the next generation of submarines and missiles and offer assistance in enriching uranium for future warheads, The Daily Telegraph said, adding that similar talks are being held with France.
The DPA news agency said earlier, citing sources in the German government, that Germany and France were taking initial practical steps as part of their nuclear deterrence cooperation. In particular, German troops are reportedly planned to take part in nuclear maneuvers in France this fall. Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev told TASS earlier that the Russian side is concerned over the upcoming German-French drills.

articles.title: WATCH huge blasts rock ‘missile warehouse’ near Kiev

WATCH huge blasts rock ‘missile warehouse’ near Kiev
A series of massive secondary explosions has torn through a warehouse complex near Kiev following a suspected Russian drone strike, with Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky appearing to suggest that dangerous military stocks had once again been stored close to populated areas.
Footage circulating online on Friday night showed enormous fireballs repeatedly illuminating the sky in Kiev Region, followed by continuing detonations from the burning site.
The Russian Defense Ministry has yet to confirm the latest strikes, but it has repeatedly vowed to carry out “systematic and consistent strikes” on Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities in retaliation for Kiev’s “terrorist attacks” on Russian civilian targets.
Today at 20:35, a strike involving Geran-4 jet-powered loitering munitions targeted a warehouse complex in the village of Myla, Bucha District, Kyiv Oblast.
The facility was used by the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) as a rocket and artillery weapons depot.

The head of the local military administration, Timur Tkachenko, confirmed that the warehouse blaze was accompanied by explosions. Authorities temporarily closed a 17km stretch of the M-06 Kiev-Chop highway in both directions and urged residents to stay away and not record the aftermath.
Several open-source monitoring accounts claimed the strike took place at around 8:35pm and involved Russian jet-powered Geran-4 loitering munitions targeting a warehouse complex near the village of Milaya.
They described the facility as a Ukrainian rocket and artillery weapons depot and claimed it might have stored a newly delivered shipment of cruise missiles or Patriot interceptors.

Koretsky said he had received reports from the interior minister and the head of Ukraine’s State Emergency Service about the strike, which he said caused a fire followed by “detonation.”
But the prime minister then drew a pointed comparison with the deadly July explosion at an ammunition depot in Vishnevoye, another Kiev suburb.
“Unfortunately, we can already state that the terrible tragedy in Vishnevoye did not become a lesson,” Koretsky said. He branded making “the same mistakes” in the fifth year of the conflict “criminal negligence” and demanded that everyone responsible face “strict punishment.”
While the PM did not spell out what those repeated mistakes were, his reference appeared to point to the storage of explosive military materiel in or near populated areas.
On July 6, a Russian strike on Vishnevoye triggered massive secondary explosions at an ammunition warehouse belonging to an enterprise within Ukraine’s state defense conglomerate Ukroboronprom. Vladimir Zelensky subsequently acknowledged that the facility was an ammunition depot.
Ukraine’s Security Service later said investigators found that ammunition had been kept in warehouses unsuitable for such storage and without the required permits, including facilities in the “immediate proximity” of residential areas. Two defense-industry executives were detained on negligence charges. articles.title: Russian court sentences former Ukrainian presidential adviser Oleksii Arestovych to 11 years in absentia

Russian court sentences former Ukrainian presidential adviser Oleksii Arestovych to 11 years in absentia
The 2nd Western District Military Court in Moscow sentenced Oleksii Arestovych, a former adviser to the presidential chief of staff of Ukraine, in absentia to 11 years in prison, the independent outlet Mediazona said on August 28.
The trial lasted a single day and was held behind closed doors. The case stemmed from videos posted on March 17, 2022, in which Arestovych called for “waging a total rail war” against Russia in the occupied territories. It also included an April 8, 2022, publication about Russia’s strike on the Kramatorsk train station.
The court found Arestovych guilty of spreading “fake” claims about the Russian military and of calling for terrorism.
Arestovych resigned from the position in January 2023 and left the country after suggesting that Ukrainian air defense had shot down the Russian missile that destroyed a residential building in Dnipro. Ukraine has since opened two criminal cases against him. In May 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky imposed sanctions against Arestovych.

articles.title: Xi, Modi, Putin to meet in Kyrgyzstan: What to watch at SCO summit
articles.body:
Some of Eurasia's most powerful leaders will gather next week in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, bringing together a complicated mix of improving ties, longstanding rivalries and regional conflicts.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin will be among those attending the Sept. 1 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Heads of State summit, which marks the group's 25th anniversary.
The gathering comes amid a tentative thaw in China-India relations following years of border tensions, as India and Pakistan navigate the aftermath of their brief conflict last year.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will also attend as Tehran faces growing US economic pressure, while conflicts and instability stretching from the Middle East and Ukraine to Afghanistan are expected to feature in discussions.
The meeting also comes as SCO members seek to capitalize on shifting global economic and geopolitical dynamics by strengthening trade, transport links and economic cooperation across Eurasia.
The SCO traces its roots to the "Shanghai Five," established in 1996 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan to reduce military tensions and address border disputes following the breakup of the Soviet Union.
Uzbekistan joined when the SCO was formally established in 2001, and the grouping remained largely centered on China, Russia and Central Asia for much of its early history.
Its international profile grew significantly with its expansion. India and Pakistan became full members in 2017, followed by Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024.
For Iran, membership marked a major diplomatic opening after years of geopolitical isolation, while Belarus's accession reflected its broader pivot toward non-Western partners
Today, the organization has 10 members: Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Belarus.
Turkmenistan is the only Central Asian country outside the SCO, reflecting its longstanding policy of permanent neutrality. Afghanistan and Mongolia have observer status, while dialogue partners include Türkiye, Azerbaijan and Saudi Arabia.
Together, SCO members have a population of around 3.4 billion, span a vast stretch of Eurasia and account for around 25% of global GDP.
Unlike NATO, the SCO is not a military alliance, nor is it an economic union like the EU. Instead, its consensus-based structure provides a forum for security cooperation, economic ties and diplomacy among countries that do not necessarily share the same interests.
One of the most closely watched encounters will be between Xi and Modi as Asia's two most populous countries seek to build on a tentative thaw after years of tensions over their disputed Himalayan border.
Senior Chinese and Indian officials held another round of boundary talks in Beijing on Aug. 25, agreeing to continue efforts toward a settlement and maintain stability along the frontier.
Relations deteriorated sharply after deadly border clashes in 2020, making the leaders' interactions in Bishkek an opportunity to gauge how far the recent improvement in ties has progressed.
The interaction between Xi and Putin will also offer a window into the increasingly close relationship between China and Russia and how the two powers coordinate within the SCO.
The gathering will also put the leaders of India and Pakistan in the same room just more than a year after the two nuclear-armed neighbors fought a brief conflict.
Pakistani Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif is slated to attend, bringing him together with Modi as tensions persist between the two countries, primarily over Kashmir.
Another leader to watch will be Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is scheduled to meet Putin on the sidelines of the summit, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
His visit comes as the US threatens increased secondary sanctions against countries and entities that continue doing business with Tehran.
According to the SCO Secretariat, leaders are expected to discuss major regional and international security challenges, including conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, the situation in Afghanistan and India's relations with China and Pakistan.
The organization has taken a more visible collective position in 2026 on Iran and the broader Middle East, including the Palestinian issue, calling for restraint, dialogue and political and diplomatic solutions.
At a July meeting, SCO foreign ministers expressed particular concern over developments in the Middle East and around Iran, reiterating that international conflicts should be settled through political and diplomatic means in accordance with international law and the UN Charter.
Afghanistan remains a longstanding regional priority, particularly because of concerns over terrorism, drug trafficking and cross-border security.
Ukraine is also expected to feature in discussions, though there has been no indication that the war will be a separate focus of the summit.
Relations between India and China and India and Pakistan are also expected to be discussed, bringing some of the SCO's own internal tensions onto the agenda.
Counterterrorism remains a core area of cooperation through the SCO's Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure, based in Tashkent. The summit is expected to approve its plans for the coming year, including possible joint exercises.
Economic connectivity will be another major focus, with transport infrastructure and a proposed SCO Development Bank among the projects under discussion.
One major transport project involving SCO members is the 7,200-kilometer (4,474-mile) International North-South Transport Corridor, which links St. Petersburg with Mumbai through Iran and ports on the Persian Gulf.
The organization also agreed in 2025 to establish a network of Silk Road Stations to support international freight traffic across Eurasia.
Members are meanwhile continuing talks on establishing an SCO Development Bank. A fourth round of consultations was held in Shenzhen in June, though its structure and operating arrangements remain under negotiation.
The SCO enters its second quarter-century as economic activity shifts toward Asia, supply chains are reconfigured and countries seek new trade and diplomatic partnerships.
For some members, it offers a platform to strengthen regional security. For others, it provides opportunities to expand economic ties, develop transport links and coordinate positions on international issues.
The summit is expected to produce a Bishkek Declaration marking the SCO's 25th anniversary, alongside documents on the organization's development and regional and international issues.
It will also mark the end of Kyrgyzstan's chairmanship and the handover to Pakistan, which is set to lead the organization for the next year and host the 2027 leaders' summit.
The SCO lacks the binding commitments of a military alliance or economic union, but its scale has made it an increasingly significant forum for dialogue across Eurasia.
As leaders gather in Bishkek for its 25th anniversary, the summit underscores how an organization founded to resolve border disputes has grown into a major multilateral grouping.
Its next challenge will be turning that scale into influence while maintaining consensus among an increasingly diverse membership.

articles.title: CIA chief’s Moscow trip puts NATO concerns in focus
articles.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe met Russian foreign intelligence chief Sergei Naryshkin during an unannounced visit to Moscow this week, as conflicting accounts emerged over whether he carried a U.S. warning against any Russian move on NATO territory.
Naryshkin, who heads Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), confirmed on Aug. 27 that the two had held a “working-level meeting” and discussed unspecified sensitive matters within the remit of their agencies.
He said there was nothing unusual about the contact.
The visit first came to public attention after flight-tracking data showed a U.S. military C-17 transport aircraft flying from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to Latvia and then Moscow’s Vnukovo airport on Aug. 25.
The Kremlin later confirmed that Ratcliffe had met Russian intelligence officials. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the talks but had not met the CIA director.
“Contacts through intelligence-service channels are in themselves a positive development, a positive process,” Peskov said.
He added that it was too early to assess whether the meeting would help improve broader relations between Moscow and Washington.
U.S. President Donald Trump described the trip as “semi-routine” during an interview with radio host Glenn Beck.
“We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said, rejecting suggestions that Ratcliffe had traveled to Moscow over possible Russian action against NATO or to seek support for U.S. pressure on Iran.
The Wall Street Journal and CBS News, citing people briefed on the visit, reported that Ratcliffe had warned Moscow against attacking a NATO member.
Trump later told Axios that no such warning had been delivered and called the trip “standard business.”
The Kremlin also dismissed the reports as “scare stories.”
The speculation followed a Wall Street Journal report on U.S. intelligence assessments that Russian President Vladimir Putin could seek to test NATO’s resolve within the next few years through measures ranging from a cyberattack to a limited military incursion.
The available information was insufficient to conclude that Moscow had a specific plan to intervene in the Baltic states.
However, a limited or initially ambiguous security incident could test how quickly NATO members reach a common assessment and agree on a response under Article 5.
Ukraine and Iran were also cited in media reports as possible subjects of the Moscow meeting, but neither side has disclosed the agenda.
Ratcliffe is the first CIA director known to have visited Moscow since William Burns traveled there in November 2021, three months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: South Korea cleared for 103 AIM-9X missiles
articles.body:
The United States has approved a possible $125 million Foreign Military Sale to South Korea covering 103 AIM-9X Sidewinder Block II air-to-air missiles, additional guidance units and associated support, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The US Department of State announced the determination on 21 August under Foreign Military Sales transmittal 26-78. The package requested by the Republic of Korea includes 103 AIM-9X Sidewinder Block II tactical missiles and ten AIM-9X Block II Tactical Guidance Units.
Associated equipment and services would include active optical target detectors, training, weapon-system support, training aids and devices, spare parts and US Government and contractor engineering, technical and logistics support.
The estimated value of the complete package is $125 million. As with other Foreign Military Sales notifications, the figure represents the estimated value of the proposed programme rather than necessarily the value of any eventual contract.
The State Department said the proposed sale would support US foreign policy and national security objectives through South Korea’s role as an American ally in the Indo-Pacific. It also said the weapons would expand the country’s air-defence capability and support interoperability with US forces.
In its notification, the department stated that the sale would “help improve the Republic of Korea’s capability to meet current and future threats by expanding its air defense capability, deterring aggression in the region, and ensuring interoperability with U.S. Forces.”
It added: “The Republic of Korea will have no difficulty absorbing these articles and services into its armed forces.”
The AIM-9X is the current generation of the Sidewinder family of short-range infrared-guided air-to-air missiles used by the United States and a number of allied air forces. The Block II version incorporates updated guidance and electronics compared with earlier variants and is designed for employment from compatible fighter aircraft using both traditional and high-off-boresight engagements.
South Korea already operates a substantial fleet of US-designed combat aircraft, including the F-15K Slam Eagle, KF-16 and F-35A Lightning II, alongside domestically developed types. The country continues to modernise its combat-air inventory while maintaining close operational links with US forces stationed on the Korean Peninsula and elsewhere in the region.
The principal contractor identified for the proposed sale is RTX Corporation, headquartered in Arlington, Virginia. The State Department said it was not currently aware of any offset agreement associated with the potential programme, with any such arrangement to be determined separately between the purchaser and contractor.

articles.title: Sweden to deploy fighter jets, warships to Finland amid fears of 'deteroriating security situation'
articles.body:
Sweden's military will participate in the surveillance and protection of Finland's territory with Gripen fighter jets and a corvette warship, at least until the end of 2026, Finland's defense forces said on Friday.
"The Swedish equipment strengthens air surveillance in particular, releasing the Finnish Defense Forces' own resources for repelling violations and incidents, if need be," Finland's military said in a statement.
The neighboring countries, NATO's two newest members, already have close bilateral defense cooperation. Finland has a 1,340-kilometer (833-mile) long eastern border with Russia.
"Sweden has responded to a request from Finland to strengthen its air defense due to the deteriorating security situation," Sweden's Defence Minister Pal Jonson told Reuters, adding that the Swedish armed forces may under the agreement, if necessary, help Finland repel violations of Finnish territory.
Besides fighter jets and vessels with drone combat capabilities, Sweden may also contribute ground-based anti-drone systems, he said.
Countries fear Russia-Ukraine war is spilling over borders
Military drones straying into the airspace of Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are stoking concerns that the war in Ukraine is spilling over into NATO's northern borders with Russia. As Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian Baltic Sea oil shipping ports, some of its drones have missed their targets and led to security warnings in neighboring countries.
Sweden's SAAB, the maker of Gripen, said separately on Friday it had won a 1.2 billion crown ($126 million) order from Finland for its RBS 70 NG portable air defense missile system.

articles.title: Russian officer killed in St. Petersburg car bombing identified as Sergei Sechkov, whose unit Ukraine accuses of strikes on civilians
articles.body:
The person killed in the Aug. 27 car explosion in St. Petersburg has been identified as 43-year-old Russian serviceman Sergei Sechkov, according to Ukrainian Telegram channel Supernova+. Sechkov’s father confirmed to the independent outlet Agentstvo that his son had died in the bombing.
A number of known details about Sechkov match information about the victim that were previously reported by Russian media. According to 78.ru, the victim was a native of Ryazan named “Sergei S.,” and his wife, who was injured in the explosion, was named Anna. According to leaked data reviewed by Agentstvo, Sechkov was 43 years old, was born in Ryazan, and his wife’s name is Anna. In addition, Sechkov’s registered address is located roughly a hundred meters from the site of the explosion.
The Ukrainian project Myrotvorets has a profile for Sergei Sergeevich Sechkov on its website, listing him with the rank of major in military unit 12633 — the 332nd Separate Guards Helicopter Regiment, part of the 6th Air Force and Air Defense Army. The St. Petersburg outlet Fontanka had previously written that the victim served in the Air Force and Air Defense troops, but referred to him as a lieutenant colonel.
In May 2022, Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) stated that servicemen of the 332nd Separate Guards Helicopter Regiment had taken part in the war against Ukraine. The HUR accused the unit of carrying out missile and bomb strikes on civilians in the Slobozhanske sector.
The car explosion in question took place on the morning of Aug. 27 near a store on Kolpinskoye Highway in the Slavyanka neighborhood of St. Petersburg. The serviceman inside the car was killed, and his wife was injured and hospitalized. The St. Petersburg office of the Investigative Committee confirmed the serviceman’s death and reported that a criminal case had been opened “over the car catching fire,” without specifying the charge.
Fontanka claims that a 24-year-old Russian woman planted the homemade explosive device under the car. According to the outlet’s account, on the evening of Aug. 26 she attached the device to the underside of the car beneath the driver’s seat, then headed to Pulkovo Airport and departed for Turkey at around five o’clock in the morning — a few hours before the explosion. Allegedly, she subsequently moved on to Chișinău, Moldova. The outlet does not name her or disclose the source of this information. Russian law enforcement agencies have not made any official statements about a search for a suspect.
The Ukrainian side has not confirmed involvement in the explosion, and no one has claimed responsibility for it.
Earlier, 78.ru reported that the victim had told his superiors he was “on a kill list.”

articles.title: From the Gripen sale to coast guard boats—Sweden sends 10 vessels to Ukraine
articles.body:
Sweden will transfer 10 coast guard boats to Ukraine, the Swedish government announced on 27 August 2026. Stockholm will also direct additional funds to multilateral defense programs for Kyiv.
Russia's full-scale invasion added to some 13,500 km² of Ukraine's rivers, lakes, and Black Sea coastline now potentially contaminated with explosive remnants of war, in the world's most mined country, and emergency service divers had cleared 190 km² of it by November 2025. Allied nations have committed billions in military support to Kyiv since 2022, from fighter jets to anti-drone systems.
Rescue boats for Ukraine's mined waterways
Ukraine's State Emergency Service will receive the work and high-speed vessels in their current condition, after the coast guard removes their markings and equipment. The agency will use them for waterborne rescue operations, including clearing mines from river channels.
Sweden detains Russians who “camped” near home of CEO of Gripen jets Ukraine is buying
Sweden's Civil Defense Minister Carl-Oskar Bohlin said Sweden is further strengthening Ukraine's maritime capabilities. He described towage, mine clearance, and transport as important capabilities that can now increase further. Sweden's Civil Defense Agency will handle transporting the boats to Ukraine.
The donation follows Sweden's broader naval support for Kyiv. In January 2025, Stockholm doubled its pledge of CB90 assault boats for Ukraine's navy to 32 and added 23 naval combat modules to arm them. The coast guard vessels serve a different purpose—rescue and utility work for a civilian agency, not combat operations.
Another $28 million for defense funds
Sweden will also channel 270 million Swedish kronor (about $28 million) to multilateral defense funds supporting Ukraine, mainly for air defense. Of that sum, $14 million goes to the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), to which Sweden contributed $108 million in June. Allies and partners fund high-priority American materiel through the US-led, NATO-administered program, and this package covers advanced air defense systems and ammunition for Kyiv.
The government said this marks Sweden's fifth PURL contribution. With the new payment, Stockholm's total PURL funding reaches $552 million.
In July, Sweden's defense minister confirmed Ukraine may use the Meteor missiles promised with its Gripen fighters against Russian aircraft over Russian territory.

articles.title: Russia destroyed last of Kherson’s heat and power equipment on 26 August. Ukraine’s new defense minister arrived days later
articles.body:
Ukraine's new defense minister went to Kherson Oblast days after Russia destroyed the heat of its main city. Yevhenii Khmara visited the region and met the head of the regional military administration, Oleksandr Prokudin, to discuss the region's most urgent needs, the Defense Ministry reported.
Russia hit the Kherson combined heat and power plant with a glide bomb on 26 August, then struck it again overnight with four more, destroying all the heat- and power-generating equipment that remained, Naftogaz said.
Prokudin has urged residents to leave, warning the city may go without heat and power through the winter. He said that Russia has dropped 170 glide bombs on the oblast since 1 July, more than in the entire first half of 2026.
Air defense topped the agenda
Khmara and Prokudin discussed strengthening defenses against various types of drones and protection against aerial bombs, as well as the safety of roads and critical infrastructure, which are being attacked by Russians day and night. They also addressed giving troops in this direction more capacity to strike the Russian targets that threaten civilians and soldiers.
The needs match the threat Prokudin has described. No region of Ukraine currently has the means to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds or glide bombs, he said, and Russia has begun using both more heavily against Kherson's infrastructure.
The minister met marines and the wounded
Khmara spoke with commanders and troops of the 30th Marine Corps operating on the Prydniprovskyi direction, the ministry said. The talks covered financial support for combat units and larger purchases of strike systems.
"We have taken up the soldiers' requests that need Defense Ministry decisions," the ministry said.
Khmara also visited a medical facility treating wounded troops and presented state awards.
The ministry frames it as direct contact
The Defense Ministry said it plans to keep working directly with troops and the leadership of front-line regions to strengthen the Defense Forces and protect Ukrainian lives.
