articles.title: There is no proof that this video shows a plane crash in Tel Aviv
articles.body:
There is no proof that this video shows a plane crash in Tel Aviv
A video showing an airplane rammed into the side of a building has been circulating widely on social media. While social media users are claiming that the video shows a plane that crashed in Tel Aviv after an Iranian attack, its origin remains unknown and its authenticity highly questionable.
A video that has gone viral on X is said to show a plane crash in Tel Aviv, Israel, after an attack carried out by Iran. The footage, which has garnered more than five million views, was published on August 26 by a fake account pretending to belong to Donald Trump Jr. It is not, however, the official account of US President Donald Trump’s son.
The video shows a plane crashed into the side of a building. The person filming the scene speaks in Russian, saying: “Just now, a plane crashed into a building. Look, it’s stuck there. It’s a huge passenger jet; the windows shattered. My god, this is really happening. I don’t know how long it will hold.”
According to the posts featuring the video, the footage was filmed in Tel Aviv and shows the aftermath of an Iranian attack. However, there is no proof that such an attack actually took place.
No sign of a crash in Tel Aviv
It turns out, this video was already posted online back in March 2026 by the pro-Iranian account Asif Ali. This is the first clue that the video might not be authentic. When we carried out an online search using the keywords “plane crash Tel Aviv”, we couldn’t find a single article about the type of crash shown in the video. No reliable media outlets reported on this crash in August 2026 or when the video was first posted online back in March 2026. When we ran a screengrab of the footage through a reverse image search (check out our handy guide here), we saw that the video hadn’t been shared by any reliable media outlets.
The official X accounts run by the Israeli authorities as well as the city of Tel Aviv also didn’t share anything about a plane crash like the one shown in this footage at any point in 2026 or in previous years.
A video likely generated by AI
The exact origin of this video is difficult to establish. It was also shared back in April 2026 with the same description, but, once again, no trustworthy source was able to confirm its origin.
There are several visual and sonic clues that the video was generated by artificial intelligence.
First of all, there is a crowd of observers gathered in an extremely questionable security area, which seems to have been marked by the authorities using yellow tape. It is directly below part of the plane that seems like it could collapse at any minute and doesn’t align with the security measures usually taken when this type of accident occurs.
Next, if you compare this fire truck to the vehicles used by fire services in Tel Aviv, it is quite different. It doesn’t have the yellow stripes you usually see on fire trucks in Tel Aviv.
Finally, there are no logos or any other distinctive elements on the plane that would help us determine what company it belongs to. This clue, along with the others we identified, suggests that the video was created by artificial intelligence.
When we ran the video through Hiya, a tool for detecting audio produced by AI, it concluded that it was 99% likely that the video’s sound was generated by artificial intelligence.
The latest strikes against Israel were reported on June 7, 2026, when several Iranian missiles were fired towards Israel for the first time since the ceasefire. There is no proof of a link between the video and a new strike on Tel Aviv.
This article has been translated from the original in French by Brenna Daldorph.

articles.title: USS North Carolina leaves dry dock after overhaul
articles.body:
Virginia-class attack submarine USS North Carolina has left dry dock at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard after completing the dry-dock phase of a scheduled maintenance and modernisation period.
The submarine, designated SSN 777, was undocked on 12 August at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility in Hawaii. It has now shifted to a pier-side berth, where work will continue ahead of its eventual return to operational service.
The US Navy said the submarine had undergone restoration and modernisation work during the dry-dock period, with the undocking marking completion of that portion of the maintenance programme.
USS North Carolina is homeported at Pearl Harbor and assigned to Submarine Squadron 1. Commissioned on 3 May 2008, the boat was the fourth Virginia-class submarine to enter service and is the fourth US Navy vessel to carry the name of the state of North Carolina.
Project supervisor Khonsa Phommavong said in the Navy release that cooperation between the shipyard workforce and the submarine’s crew had been central to keeping the programme moving.
Phommavong said: “Cmdr. Fritts’ leadership fostered an environment of standards and expectations, complete transparency, and mutual accountability. By maintaining an open dialogue regarding daily priorities and risks, he ensured that both the ship’s force and our civilians were aligned on the same mission, effectively eliminating silos and driving us toward a unified goal.”
Commander Michael Fritts, commanding officer of USS North Carolina, said the submarine had been undocked on schedule despite the complexity involved in a major overhaul.
Fritts said: “I’m extremely proud of my crew, the A77 Project Team, and Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard for undocking North Carolina on time.”
He added: “Our teams have overcome many challenges due to the complexity of a major overhaul; however, thanks to strong collaboration, we have kept our availability schedule on track. True to its ‘No Ka Oi’ (the best) motto, PHNSY continues to set the standard for excellence.”
The Virginia class forms the current backbone of US Navy nuclear-powered attack submarine construction. Boats of the class are designed for missions including anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare, land attack, intelligence gathering and support for special operations forces.
According to the Navy, USS North Carolina is capable of conducting anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare, strike missions, special operations support and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.
Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard carries out maintenance, repair and modernisation work on US Navy submarines and surface ships in the Pacific. Its location in Hawaii makes it a major maintenance facility between the US West Coast and forward operating areas in the western Pacific.
Shipyard commander Captain Ryan McCrillis said in the release: “Returning a critical asset like North Carolina back to the fleet is a massive accomplishment, but the real story is the dedication of the people who made it happen.”
He added: “The strength and spirit of aloha this workforce has is immense. It drives our people to support one another, face every demanding shift together, and pour their pride into this mission.”
The submarine’s departure from dry dock does not mark the completion of the overall maintenance period. Pier-side work and operational preparations remain before the boat can return to active fleet operations.
Phommavong said: “When I look back at the effort invested to get North Carolina ready for undocking, what makes me most proud is the unwavering commitment and dedication of our people. It’s very motivating.”
USS North Carolina will continue its maintenance availability alongside the pier at Pearl Harbor as the shipyard and crew work through the remaining stages required before the submarine returns to operational status with the Pacific Fleet.

articles.title: Slovak Police Foil Possible Napalm Attack on Factory Producing Drones for Ukraine
articles.body:
Reported by
Officers from ÚBOK—Slovakia’s Office for the Fight Against Organized Crime—thwarted a potential arson attack on the Skyeton factory near Prešov, which manufactures unmanned systems for the Ukrainian military, police announced earlier this week.
The Ukrainian company's Raybird-3 drones can stay airborne for up to 28 hours and travel up to 2,500 kilometers, operating deep behind enemy lines.
Had the attack succeeded, police said, it would have risked a large-scale fire, endangered the roughly 70 employees who could have been on site, and caused damage worth tens of millions of dollars.
The Slovak Information Service and Military Intelligence played a key role in uncovering the plot, providing information that prompted ÚBOK to launch an intensive investigation. Police identified the perpetrators before the attack could take place and seized a large quantity of incendiary mixture—identified by the Police Force's Institute of Forensic Science as a blend of gasoline and polystyrene commonly known as napalm—along with tools, a mobile phone, an action camera and a hand-drawn plan of the attack.
Three foreign nationals were charged with preparing an especially serious crime of general endangerment, committed as accomplices for hire. Two were detained in Slovakia. German authorities arrested the third under a European arrest warrant issued in an exceptionally short time. Their identities and nationalities have not been made public yet.
When asked for comment, Román Hájek, a spokesperson for the Police Force Presidium, said investigators moved quickly once the tip came in, launching an immediate operational search effort that allowed them to identify those involved before any damage was done. He said officers from the regional police directorate in Prešov also provided significant support during the operation.
"Thanks to the timely intervention of police, no one was injured, and no property damage occurred," Hájek said. He added that the investigation is ongoing and that a change in the case's legal classification has not been ruled out.
In comments to Ukrainian media Skyeton accused Russia of orchestrating the sabotage, noting that Moscow regularly targets the company's domestic facilities as well as its reputation.
"The recent attempted attack on our facility in Slovakia is further proof that Ukrainian defense manufacturers have become a real thorn in their side, and that we are on the right path," the company said.
The case lands amid heightened concern across Europe over sabotage targeting firms tied to Ukraine's defense supply chain, with security officials increasingly describing such plots—often involving foreign nationals recruited for hire—as part of a broader pattern of hybrid attacks reaching well beyond the war's front lines.

articles.title: Drones attack thermal power plant in Shchastia, causing major blackout in Russian-occupied territories
articles.body:
Drones attack thermal power plant in Shchastia, causing major blackout in Russian-occupied territories
A major blackout occurred on the night of 27-28 August across temporarily occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. The power cuts followed a drone attack on the Luhansk Thermal Power Plant in the city of Shchastia.
Source: a Russian media outlet Astra; monitoring Telegram channels
Details: Local sources began warning of a possible drone attack as early as 21:00 on 27 August.
Around midnight, posts on social media about power outages began appearing in large numbers. In particular, the power went off in occupied Donetsk at around 01:00 on 28 August.
Local residents reported that the drone strike had caused a fire at the thermal power plant in Shchastia. Photos were also posted online that reportedly showed a fire at the facility.
Shortly afterwards, reports of widespread power outages began coming in from the so-called Donetsk People's Republic and occupied parts of Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. Meanwhile, local Telegram channels said there was "no precise or official information".
For reference: Russian forces fully occupied the city of Shchastia on 28 February 2022. After seizing the city, the Russians announced the so-called "nationalisation" of the power plant. They used the plant's generating units to cover the power shortfall in the so-called Luhansk People's Republic.
The Luhansk Thermal Power Plant is also a key facility supporting Russia's defence industry in Ukraine's east. The plant supplies electricity to military bases, repair facilities, coal mines and railway infrastructure used by the Russian military to supply its forces.

articles.title: WHO reports more than 3,200 attacks on Ukraine’s healthcare system since full-scale invasion
articles.body:
WHO reports more than 3,200 attacks on Ukraine’s healthcare system since full-scale invasion
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, 3,205 attacks on healthcare facilities have been carried out, World Health Organization (WHO) Representative for Ukraine Jarno Habicht reported on Friday following fresh overnight strikes.
Key points
- Attacks on humanitarian warehouses in Ukraine have destroyed medical supplies meant for hundreds of thousands of people
- Despite the dangers, WHO and UN partners continue delivering aid to hard-to-reach areas while supporting Ukrainian healthcare workers facing severe psychological strain
- Fresh overnight attacks killed at least 12 civilians and damaged more aid warehouses, prompting renewed UN calls for a ceasefire
Such attacks undermine the ability of humanitarian organizations to provide support to people in need.
“In 2026, 20 attacks on warehouses containing humanitarian aid have already been recorded, including 13 warehouses where medical supplies were stored,” Dr, Habicht said.
“WHO faced similar attacks in Kyiv in July and Dnipro in August, resulting in the loss of significant amounts of medicine and equipment intended to help 225,000 people,” he added.
Despite the difficult and dangerous conditions, WHO and its partners continued to deliver humanitarian aid, provide consultations and support the Ukrainian healthcare system.
Delivering in hard-to-reach areas
So far this year, nine WHO humanitarian convoys and 22 UN inter-agency convoys, including two that departed for the Donetsk region on Friday, delivered medicines, equipment and other medical supplies to more than 50 settlements in hard-to-reach areas.
With WHO support, primary health care teams have provided 13,130 consultations in seven regions of Ukraine over the past eight months.
In areas where pharmacies are not operating, 28,400 people received over-the-counter drug kits this year.
“As part of WHO’s comprehensive humanitarian response, we supported the health system by providing equipment and supplies to more than 300 health facilities – including primary health care centres, hospitals, laboratories and transit points – enabling them to help three million people,” Dr. Habicht said.
Medical staff face enormous stress
The WHO representative also said that the war is placing a heavy burden on Ukrainian medical workers.
A recent WHO study found that more than one quarter of doctors and nurses reported symptoms consistent with depressive disorder, and one in five health workers exhibited signs of anxiety disorder.
“Our task is to implement additional measures and support tools for those who help people and save lives,” said Dr. Habicht.
To support the psychological wellbeing of healthcare workers, WHO has incorporated elements of psychological first aid and self-care skills into ambulance crew training programs. More than 40 specialists from 11 regions have completed the training.
The organization also runs a programme for primary healthcare and rehabilitation professionals, with more than 700 healthcare workers taking part.
Participants demonstrated significant improvements in psychological wellbeing and performance as well as a reduction in symptoms of stress, depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
Preparing for winter
Dr. Habicht warned that Ukraine faces another difficult winter, and WHO is doing everything possible to help Ukrainians prepare for the cold season.
To ensure the smooth operation of medical services, the UN health agency has already installed 30 heating systems in medical facilities.
Another 22 are planned for installation before winter, WHO said.
Part of wider pattern
Authorities say attacks across Ukraine between yesterday and the early hours of this morning have killed at least 12 civilians and injured more than 65 others, with frontline regions were especially hard hit, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Friday.
Other UN agencies are reporting fresh attacks on its aid storage sites, including the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), which said strikes in the Kyiv region hit one its warehouses, destroying humanitarian supplies that will hamper the delivery of vital assistance ahead of winter.
“This is part of a wider pattern, with at least six warehouses belonging to humanitarian operations impacted by attacks in Ukraine in this month,” Mr. Dujarric said.
“We reiterate, once again, the Secretary-General’s condemnations of large-scale missile and drone attacks by the armed forces of the Russian Federation in urban centres in Ukraine,” the UN Spokesperson said, reiterating the UN chief’s call for an urgent de-escalation, leading to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire.

articles.title: Leaders Pivoting on Data Centers Require More Than Roads, Water, and Power Promises
articles.body:
Data center companies “dug their own grave,” Texas Governor Greg Abbott said Sunday, and “that’s why they got the backlash they deserve.” Nine months ago, Abbott crowned Texas the epicenter of AI development, alongside Google executives announcing a $40 billion investment in the state. 
Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro, a Democrat who actively recruited Amazon’s $20 billion commitment to his commonwealth, made a similar U-turn days earlier, signing an executive order he calls the “nation’s strictest guardrails” on data centers: no more fast-track permits, no nondisclosure agreements, and no state permit review until developers make binding commitments to community standards.
When a Texas Republican and a Pennsylvania Democrat pivot to the same position in the same week, it becomes clear that the politics of data centers have shifted. Like everything else in AI, sentiment is moving at an extraordinary pace. Even the AI industry’s biggest winner recognizes the need for change. The tech sector needs to “do a much better job working with the communities,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said this week.
While shifting or walking back public statements never looks good, leaders are simply listening to voters’ demands. The truth is that leaders across the political spectrum are pivoting on data centers for a simple reason: they want their communities to actually benefit. The best ones are listening to citizens’ concerns while constructively raising the bar for the data center industry—not cutting them off.
The costs and benefits of data centers
Seven in ten Americans tell Gallup they oppose a data center in their own community, more opposition than a nuclear plant draws. The primary complaint started with electric bills. PJM’s independent market monitor attributes 63% of the region’s 2025/2026 capacity price increase to data center load, roughly $9.3 billion recovered from customers across 13 states in a single year, causing household bills to rise 1.5% to 5% this summer.
The countervailing benefits are just as measurable. In Loudoun County, Virginia (often referred to as known as the "Data Center Capital of the World”), data centers supply as much as 31% of local revenue by the state legislature’s audit count, and the county has banked a $119.7 million stabilization fund against any downturn. The facilities also pay blue-collar wage premiums of 10% to 64% over comparable employers, the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz finds in Indeed postings data. The Dallas Fed has reported that skilled concrete workers, who typically make $28 to $32 per hour, are earning $45 per hour and a $150 per diem on data center jobs. And in July, the National Federation of Independent Business found that small-business optimism is at its highest levels in a year, crediting AI investment in chips and the structures that house them with spillover business opportunities.
The fight over data centers, meanwhile, has become a social and political flashpoint and, at times, embellished beyond what the record supports. Some backlash is earned. Most jobs promised are temporary. Resource demands are massive, and draining when mismanaged. Speculators have gamed interconnection queues and incentive programs, while both developers and policymakers have done a poor job communicating to the public. We heard these concerns from over 50 mayors leading cities that span the U.S. during our annual Yale Mayors College in March.
Done well, though, these projects are a once-in-a-generation development opportunity for places ranging from underused farmland to urban brownfield sites. As Huang explained it: “This is the first time in probably the last century that we’re able to invest in sustainable energy, invest in improving our energy grid, securing our energy supply, reducing the cost of energy across the country.”
Local and federal responses
Opposition to data centers tends to concentrate at the county level because costs pool locally while benefits disperse. A county absorbs the water draw, the noise, the land conversion, and a share of the regional capacity bill. The compute serves users elsewhere, and the returns accrue to shareholders nowhere nearby. Every serious policy response attempts to move some portion of that diffuse benefit back to the community bearing the concentrated cost.
The responses span a diverse spectrum. New York paused state environmental permitting on large data centers for at least one year, pending a statewide study—the only statewide pause in effect, for now. Texas ordered an audit of every project in its grid queue, and the state’s grid operator paused new data center connections until the audit is complete. Maine’s legislature passed the first statewide construction moratorium this spring, only for Governor Janet Mills to veto the bill and create an advisory council to write standards instead. More broadly, 27 states advanced large-load legislation this year, with California, Ohio, and Utah enacting laws that exceed the industry’s voluntary ratepayer pledge to the White House.
At the federal level, Washington continues to accelerate. A July 2025 executive order fast-tracked federal permitting, and a December preemption order, whose promised list of invalid state laws has yet to appear, expressly preserved state authority over “AI compute and data center infrastructure, other than generally applicable permitting reforms.”
Beneath the surface, the two sides are searching for a shared premise: the buildout must take the form of a mutually beneficial, transparent partnership. The public is already there. In Morning Consult polling commissioned for our June CEO Summit, 55% of Americans view data centers as a community benefit, while 69% call the backlash justified, the clearest indicator of an electorate searching for better terms, not fewer projects.
“Don’t ban—raise the bar, ask for more,” suggests Chris Crosby, CEO of Compass Datacenters.
Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg drew the same position in his August letter, proposing a community compact of local jobs, investment in schools, and public services, held-down energy prices, and environmental care, backed by a $1 billion fund. When the company told Eagle Mountain, Utah, back in 2018 that it wanted to be a welcomed corporate partner, local public leaders answered, “Well, then we’re going to ask for some things.” And ask they did.
Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, whose state hosts more data centers than any other, has taken note and come to define the state’s role as ensuring “our local communities know what they can ask for and what standards they should be setting.” If knowing what to ask for is half the problem, then capacity to execute is the other half. The table often seats a county planning staff of a dozen across from a trillion-dollar counterparty, and that imbalance has unfortunately appeared in lopsided deals negotiated behind nondisclosure agreements.
Yet the smaller side of the table holds more leverage today than it may realize. The industry is desperate to scale and willing to deal. “AI is constrained today by data center capacity, not compute or software,” MARA Holdings CEO Fred Thiel tells us.
In reviewing the tariffs, statutes, audits, agreements, and published commitments behind the American AI buildout and other noteworthy economic development projects for our forthcoming book When Machines Act, we identified those practices that have produced win-win outcomes for all parties.
Pay full freight, and sign for the total
Our research suggests that major industry players have already accepted the central demand from communities. Data centers should pay the full grid costs of their own growth, and industry committed to do so when seven of them, from Amazon to xAI, signed the White House ratepayer pledge in March. Anthropic, though not among the signatories, also committed weeks earlier to cover the electricity price increases, transmission lines, and substations its own data centers require. “This should be the expectation across the industry,” the company wrote. Microsoft went even further, telling regulators to set rates high enough so that data center costs do not impact anyone else.
A pledge is only as good as the paper behind it, which is why Google’s Capacity Commitment Framework matters as much as any of them—a structure that includes guaranteed minimums, a security deposit, and cancellation fees a utility can collect. Water has followed the same path from promise to specification. Microsoft is aiming for a 40% improvement in datacenter water-use intensity by 2030, and Meta has pledged to restore double what it consumes in stressed watersheds.
Flexible demand response is another potential lever few contracts have adopted and is one of the cheapest options available. Duke’s Nicholas Institute calculates that if data centers trimmed their peak demand just 1% to 2%, retail electricity prices could fall as much as 2.8%. Utilities build power plants and wires to cover the few highest-demand hours of the year, so a data center that briefly tempers or shifts computing during those hours reduces the amount of new generation and transmission that must be built. The avoided construction flows through regulated rates as savings to every customer. Operators can avoid performance losses—shifting tasks in time or place during peak periods—and save up to $8.00 per megawatt-hour for their contribution.
Trade tax breaks for assets that last
Incentives are a different matter, costing taxpayers real money, so the first question for any state is whether a subsidy changes a company’s decision. Georgia’s independent state audit found that the sales-tax exemption changed the siting decision for roughly 30% of data center activity, and while the incentive produced a net fiscal loss of $433 million in fiscal 2025, it also returned $2.86 in economic value across the broader economy per dollar forgone. While critics carry the loss and boosters the multiplier, the audit’s real lesson belongs to neither camp. A state that pays for 10 projects to decide only three should be asking for far more than it does.
A study by the Brookings Institution finds that hyperscale sitings follow power, land, and fiber, meaning subsidies largely pay for what was coming anyway. The smarter deal asks the incoming project to fund assets the community keeps, such as transmission upgrades, roads, and water systems, that compound in value over the long run.
Compass Datacenters’ Crosby volunteers that rationale himself. On a $5 billion project, spending $100 million on transmission upgrades “makes a lot of sense to me from a real estate perspective.” Taking a page from semiconductor industrial policy—such as Micron conditioning its Central New York megafab on a $500 million community fund shaped by 300 local civic groups—states can require data center operators to seed long-term local endowments. And New Jersey is conditioning AI data center credits on partnerships with in-state universities and startups, converting a tax break into innovation-economy seed capital.
Write the rules before the applications arrive
Seed capital compounds only where the rules were written before the arrival of the applications. Eagle Mountain set expectations first and approvals second. Meta spent roughly $100 million on roads and electrical service before construction, backed a creek restoration project the city expects to return 476 million gallons of water a year, and granted more than $1 million to local schools and nonprofits. The company is carrying that playbook forward to Hyperion, its largest campus yet, in Richland Parish, Louisiana, where it has pledged more than $1 billion for local roads, water, and wastewater systems and funded data center trade scholarships for every parish high school graduate—and where surging parish tax receipts funded $50,000 teacher bonuses this year.
Yet both campuses also carried confidentiality and nondisclosure agreements that cast a shadow over the goodwill earned from community investments. Data centers need to deal transparently and operate openly, since closed-door agreements breed suspicion even when the terms are generous.
Public verification, therefore, matters as much as a pledge to a long-term partnership. The city of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, publicly posted its full agreement with a data center consortium, secured the obligations with a letter of credit, and bound the counterparties to the land, all while granting no city tax breaks. Georgia’s audit process exists because of a requirement from a 2024 transparency statute. New York attaches a uniform per-megawatt host fee to large renewable projects—a renewable-siting design that data center statutes could borrow—and researchers studying the first twenty projects under the law found the fee became a floor that communities negotiated above. From another parallel case, Massachusetts addresses the root of the asymmetry by allowing the gaming commission to require casino applicants to pay the host community’s legal expenses. In policy, the standards embraced by Spanberger provide communities with the knowledge of what to ask for and how to ask for it well.
How a state sequences these tools matters as much as which it selects. States must build the accountability layer first, requiring disclosure, published agreements, and scheduled audits before offering a single incentive. The negotiated package of local benefits that Lancaster and Eagle Mountain modeled (host community frameworks) and the rate design that binds a data center to the full grid costs the industry has pledged (cost-coverage tariffs) should then pair local benefits and ratepayer protection as one package. Any incentive that follows needs to be conditioned on a “but-for test” fortified with a proportional clawback instrument, and only then should states pilot novel concepts such as flexible demand response and ownership stakes that give host communities equity in the projects themselves.
An effective state framework
Ultimately, we have found that four universal principles govern an effective state framework:
- Commitment prior to permitting: Binding community and grid compacts must precede site approvals.
- Proportionality: Infrastructure and community asks must scale directly with peak megawatt demand.
- Enforceable security: Pledges must be backed by letters of credit, escrow reserves, or parent-company guarantees.
- Statewide baseline floors: Establish statewide statutory floors to prevent developers from regulatory arbitrage across county lines.
A year ago, data center developers and their backers spent little to no time on policy. Today, some, Crosby among them, are spending as much as 80% of their time on it. As he put it: “Our social license is at risk, and we have to figure that out as an industry.”
Willingness, at times, has even outrun the law’s ability to receive it. Compass Datacenters offered the Texas Public Utility Commission $100 million toward transmission upgrades but was refused because existing law did not permit the entity to accept the funding. The mismatch captures the moment. The moment is moving faster than the rules that govern, and that pace obliges data center owners and developers to work closely and transparently with the states, localities, and communities that host their projects.
When managed properly, we believe these facilities can be monumental opportunities for the towns that attract them. The buildout, in Huang’s words, “is going to re-industrialize the United States.” If the trend persists, however, the moment could be lost to neighboring nations that do embrace them, such as border towns like Tijuana, Mexico. Even more, the demand underneath them carries national weight, too, as the buildout will help decide whether America leads the AI race with China or falls behind. What remains is establishing enforceable terms that let both sides meet in the middle, so the communities hosting the infrastructure of the AI era also hold a durable share of what is built in their backyards.
In 1937, Aldous Huxley ominously warned in Ends and Means: “Technological progress has merely provided us with more efficient means for going backwards.” As communities across the nation and across parties come to embrace this neo-Luddite resistance to data centers, some developers are listening, learning, and hopefully acting.
With research assistance from Frankie Reichman and Zander Jeinthanuttkanont.

articles.title: Ukrainian robot commander calls ground robots “Persian elephants.” What army really needs are “Arabian steeds”, he says
articles.body:
A Ukrainian ground robot used to run 12-15 missions. Near Kupiansk, it now survives three or four. The lifespan is collapsing under the denser Russian FPV drone and mining fire, Andrii Kopach, call sign "Matematyk", who commands a ground-robot unit in the "Lava" unmanned regiment of the "Khartia" corps, told Oboronka.
Ground robots have become a daily part of the front in Ukraine. Ukrainian units ran 16,676 logistics, strike, and evacuation missions with them in June, up 122 percent since January, and the military has contracted more than 22,000 for 2026, nearly double the 2025 total. That scale runs into a wall at the front, where Russia now assigns FPV crews, including fiber-optic drones, specifically to kill the robots.
The lifespan keeps shrinking
The pace of technological change is the core problem, Matematyk said. Ukrainian makers keep improving the platforms, but cannot always keep pace with how quickly the fighting evolves.
A machine may last only three or four missions now, as in Kharkiv Oblast, where it was eight or nine before and 12 to 15 earlier still, he said. Mining, Russian fiber-optic activity, FPV activity, and a targeted focus on countering robots all drive the decline.
Speed is the missing requirement
Most robots at the front are technologically outdated in speed and suspension, Matematyk said. Current figures of 10 to 15 kilometers per hour no longer allow a machine to cross logistics routes safely.
He put the problem in an image. Gun-armed combat robots, he said, are "Persian elephants", fearsome but so slow to reach the objective that "a couple of centuries" pass first. What the army needs are "Arabian steeds" that gallop in, do the job, and gallop back.
AI defense is in development
Ukrainian troops are working with Brave1 and the Digital Transformation Ministry on AI-based active-protection systems that could autonomously detect and neutralize enemy FPVs, Matematyk said. The approaches vary, from a camera to a mini-radar to a camera paired with sound.
The countermeasures could be net launchers, or for fast machines, shotgun blasts and shrapnel, he said. The detection and response are trained on models built from the data his unit has logged over previous years. Ukraine still holds a quality edge over Russian robots through better Starlink-based communications and decentralized robot groups in its units, he added.

articles.title: Media outlets identify Russian serviceman killed in car blast in St Petersburg
articles.body:
Media outlets identify Russian serviceman killed by car bomb in St Petersburg
A Russian serviceman who was killed by a car bomb in St Petersburg on 27 August has been identified as Major Sergei Sechkov of the 332nd Helicopter Regiment. He was listed in the Myrotvorets database and supposedly assassinated by a 24-year-old Russian woman who had been recruited by Ukrainians. [Myrotvorets, which means "peacemaker", is a Ukrainian website that publishes a running list (and sometimes personal details) of people whom the authors consider to be enemies of Ukraine – ed.]
Source: Russian media outlets 78.ru, Fontanka.ru, Agentstvo. News and Astra; Ukrainian Telegram channels Supernova+ and Exilenova+
Quote from Supernova+: "Major Sergei Sechkov is believed to have been killed in St Petersburg yesterday. He was listed in the Myrotvorets database with the rank of major."
Details: Sechkov's father confirmed to Agentstvo.News that his son had been killed in the blast. Details of Sechkov's biography also match information published yesterday in Russian media outlets.
Another outlet, 78.ru, identified the 43-year-old serviceman killed in the blast as Sergei S., who was born in Ryazan. According to the outlet, Sechkov had told his superiors that he was on a "kill list" and regularly checked his car before setting off.
Astra reported that Sechkov and his wife, Anna, lived around 100 metres away from the scene. Anna, who was also in the car at the time of the blast, works at an online marketplace collection point near where the incident occurred. She is currently in hospital. However, an eyewitness said reports circulating in the media the previous day that both of her legs had been blown off are untrue.
Resources linked to Russian military aviation have also confirmed the death of a Russian Air Force serviceman in St Petersburg on 27 August, Exilenova+ reported.
According to the Myrotvorets website, Sechkov was registered at an address in St Petersburg and served in the 332nd Separate Guards Helicopter Regiment of the 6th Air and Air Defence Army. He took part in the war against Ukraine. Defence Intelligence of Ukraine has described servicemen from the unit as "war criminals" and accused them of attacks on civilians on the Slobozhanshchyna front.
According to Fontanka, a 24-year-old woman attached an improvised explosive device to the underside of Sechkov's car. It is alleged that representatives of the Ukrainian Armed Forces contacted her several months ago via a messaging app, convinced her that she was "living in the wrong country", and offered to arrange for her to move to Ukraine after she had carried out the task of blowing up the car.
On the evening of 26 August, according to media reports, she placed the explosive device under the driver's seat and immediately left for Pulkovo airport. By 05:00 she had flown to Türkiye.
The FSB supposedly identified her almost immediately and contacted Türkiye, asking the authorities to detain her. However, Turkish law enforcement said that she had already flown on to Chișinău, Moldova.
Background:
- On the morning of 27 August, a car exploded in St Petersburg's Pushkinsky district. The media identified its owner as a lieutenant colonel serving in Russia's Air Force and air defence units and reported that he had died and his wife had been injured.
- The Russian Investigative Committee later said the victims had been identified and confirmed that the deceased was a serviceman and the injured woman was his wife.

articles.title: Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine’s modern commercial storage capacity. Retail logistics are being reshaped
articles.body:
Russian attacks have destroyed about 90% of Ukraine’s modern facilities for storing goods, significantly disrupting the country’s retail logistics, Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said on 28 August, according to Interfax-Ukraine.
Russia has increasingly targeted Ukraine’s civilian commercial and logistics infrastructure in recent weeks, striking warehouses, distribution centers, hypermarkets, postal terminals and other facilities that keep goods moving through the country. The campaign has damaged supply chains and forced businesses to find more expensive and vulnerable ways to store and deliver products.
Vysotskyi said the destruction does not pose a threat of famine, but warned that continued Russian attacks on logistics infrastructure could affect the range of products available in Ukrainian stores. Supermarkets in Kyiv have already seen widespread empty shelves in recent weeks.
Retailers forced to change how goods are delivered
The destruction of warehouses has forced retailers to change how they move products around the country, with deliveries increasingly being made “from the wheels” rather than through conventional storage and distribution facilities, Vysotskyi said.
Such logistics are more complicated and expensive, he said, while some companies have begun relocating their operations to other areas. Russian attacks, however, have also reached some of the relocated facilities.
The comments come as Russia has increasingly targeted commercial and logistics infrastructure across Ukraine. In recent days, Russian drones have struck warehouses, hypermarkets, postal terminals and shopping centers, including in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia.
Kyiv has been under attack for 2 days nonstop. Russia is targeting the capital’s civilian supply chains
No threat of famine, minister says
Despite the scale of the destruction, Vysotskyi stressed that Ukraine does not face a food shortage severe enough to threaten the population with famine.
The main impact is expected to be on logistics, availability and the range of goods offered in stores. With fewer storage facilities, retailers have less capacity to stock products and must rely more heavily on direct deliveries.
The shift can also increase costs because goods have to move more frequently and over potentially longer routes without the buffer provided by large distribution centers.
Calls for risk-sharing after Russian strikes
Vysotskyi also called for a system to distribute the financial risks when Russian attacks destroy goods somewhere along the supply chain.
He said these losses currently fall within private contractual relationships between businesses, with the state not acting as an operator in the supply chain. In his view, the risks should be shared more fairly between companies involved in supplying and selling products.
He said such a system would not necessarily mean splitting losses equally. Different products have different margins, sales conditions and profitability, so the share of risk should depend on the specific product and terms of cooperation.
Russia’s attacks on storage and distribution infrastructure are therefore creating effects far beyond the facilities themselves. Damage to the supply chain can change what products reach stores, increase the cost of getting them there, and make Ukraine’s retail system more vulnerable to further strikes.

articles.title: Zelensky calls for Ukraine to launch 1,000 drones at Russia daily
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky called for Ukraine to increase the frequency of its long-range drone strikes against Russia on Aug. 28, setting a goal of launching 1,000 drones a day.
Zelensky said in his daily evening address that Ukraine currently launches more than 300 long-range drones on average each day, but needs to significantly increase that number as Russia intensifies its aerial attacks against Ukrainian cities.
"The main priority is to strengthen our defense against jet-powered Shaheds and to step up the frequency of our deep strikes against Russia," Zelensky said. "The task is a thousand drones for long-range strikes against Russia every day. Right now, the average is over 300 of our long-range strikes, there must be more. We have a very specific goal, and we will achieve it."
Zelensky's comments came as Ukrainian forces have stepped up attacks on Russian energy and military infrastructure.
He also pointed to growing pressure on Russia's fuel and export sectors, saying Moscow was already experiencing economic consequences from the war.
"They (Russia) already have less gasoline, fewer exports, and fewer logistics," Zelensky said. "For the first time in its history, Russia is importing gasoline and is in fact using budget funds to support its oil companies."
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian oil infrastructure as part of its long-range strike campaign. Ukrainian forces launched a strike on Aug. 28 targeting one of Russia's largest oil refineries in the Yaroslavl region. Ukrainian officials also said a Russian Tu-95 strategic bomber was damaged at Engels air base in the Saratov region.
The General Staff confirmed the target of the attack on Yaroslavl was the Slavneft-YANOS refinery, one of Russia's largest oil-processing facilities.
On Aug. 26, Ukrainian forces struck production facilities at the Lukoil-Nizhegorodorgsintez oil refinery, also known as NORSI, in Kstovo in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region. Ukraine's General Staff said the strike hit its target and caused a fire.
The overnight attack damaged several processing units, inter-unit infrastructure, and other plant facilities. The refinery subsequently halted crude oil processing.
Zelensky said Ukraine would continue expanding its long-range strikes if Russia refused to negotiate an end to the war.
"There will be even more such losses for them if Russia does not want to talk rationally about ending this war," he said.

articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 28. /TASS/. All countries, including Russia, underestimated the potential of artificial intelligence in the military sphere, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev said at the New Media Festival, citing events in recent years since the start of the special military operation.
"Everything that has happened to us in the past few years since the start of the special military operation shows that the world underestimated the potential of artificial intelligence and new means of warfare. Everyone did. And, incidentally, so did we," Medvedev said.

articles.title: More than 113,000 Russians cross into Georgia in a week as fears grow of new mobilization, Politico reports
articles.body:
More than 113,000 Russians cross into Georgia in a week as fears grow of new mobilization, Politico reports
More than 113,000 Russians crossed into Georgia via the Upper Lars checkpoint last week amid growing fears the Kremlin is preparing to announce a new mobilization wave, Politico reported on Aug. 28.
The spike in border crossings comes as the Kremlin undertakes increasingly aggressive recruitment measures, expands data collection on military reservists, and broadens the mandate for the National Guard, all of which have fueled speculation of an imminent call-up.
Earlier, Ukraine's Presidential Office issued a warning on Aug. 27, saying that Russia plans to mobilize 600,000 recruits over 2026 and 2027, with 300,000 to be called up this year and another 300,000 next year, according to a briefing from Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR).
"Russia's political leadership views an additional wave of mobilization as a response to the aggressor state's loss of the initiative in the war, the continued increase in personnel losses on the front, and the significant slowdown in contract recruitment across the regions," the Presidential Office said in a statement.
Alexey Tabalov, founder of the Russian human rights group School of the Conscript, told Politico his organization has seen a recent rise in requests for legal assistance from men of military age, "primarily from those in the military reserve."
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in early August that Ukrainian intelligence expected Russia to launch a "rapid mobilization" of several hundred thousand men by the end of the year.
Speaking to journalists earlier this week, Zelensky said Russia plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after the State Duma elections in September, but would avoid targeting major cities to minimize public backlash.
According to Zelensky, the newly mobilized troops would supplement existing recruitment inflows and could be used either to reinforce Russia's offensive on the "fortress belt" cities in Donetsk Oblast or to open new fronts elsewhere, including along Ukraine's northern border.
Georgia has seen this kind of border traffic before. In September 2022, when Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a partial mobilization that called up some 300,000 men, Georgia received more than 100,000 Russians within a week as one of the few countries bordering Russia to allow visa-free entry.
Since then, Russia has largely relied on contract soldiers to replenish its troops, while gradually expanding and developing new ways to attract recruits, including targeting university students.
The Kremlin has denied the mobilization rumors for months. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said this week that talk of a mobilization was "being planted by the Ukrainian authorities" to "ideologically destabilize the situation."

articles.title: Russia attacks Nova Poshta depot near Kyiv, strikes again as firefighters tackle blaze – photos
articles.body:
Russia attacks Nova Poshta depot near Kyiv, strikes again as firefighters tackle blaze – photos
A Russian attack on the night of 27-28 August struck a Nova Poshta logistics facility in Sviatopetrivske, part of the Bilohorodka hromada in Kyiv Oblast, also damaging a nearby production facility. Nova Poshta is Ukraine's largest private delivery company.
Source: Bilohorodka Mayor Anton Ovsiienko on Facebook; press service for Nova Poshta; State Emergency Service of Ukraine
Quote: "Another difficult night for the Bilohorodka hromada. The Nova Poshta depot in Sviatopetrivske was hit and a nearby production facility was damaged.
Information about casualties is being confirmed."
Details: Ovsiienko said that approximately an hour after the initial strike, while firefighters were tackling the blaze, two more strikes had hit the same location. The firefighters managed to move to a safer area in time.
Due to heavy smoke, residents of Sviatopetrivske and nearby areas have been urged to keep their windows closed and, if possible, avoid going outside unless necessary. Local authorities also asked people not to approach the site of the strike because of the risk of further attacks.
Update: Nova Poshta's press service reported that a sorting depot in Kyiv Oblast had been destroyed as a result of the Russian drone attack. All the company's employees are safe.
The company is currently assessing the impact of the attack. Nova Poshta said it will compensate customers for the full declared value of damaged parcels and contact each customer to provide details of the reimbursement.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said that firefighters are working at several locations in the Bucha district, which includes the Bilohorodka hromada, where drone strikes had caused fires in warehouse buildings and vehicles.
At one of the locations, a second drone strike was recorded while firefighters were working. After carrying out some reconnaissance, they resumed their work. The fire at the warehouse building was brought under control and efforts to deal with the aftermath are ongoing.
Firefighters also extinguished fires involving 13 cars. A high-rise residential building was damaged by the blast wave, with its windows shattered.
Firefighters continue to operate under the constant threat of further strikes.
Background: Russian forces struck Kyiv Oblast with attack drones and ballistic missiles on the night of 26-27 August, damaging warehouses in the Boryspil and Fastiv districts. A 15-year-old girl and a 73-year-old woman were injured.

Kremlin claims battlefield gains as Russia focuses attacks on Ukrainian books and toys
The Kremlin believes Russia's advance on the Ukrainian front is "obvious" and has dismissed talk of escalation as merely "Western scare stories". Russia has made it clear that it has no intention of abandoning its stepped-up aggression and is insisting that its demands be met.
Source: Russian media outlets, citing Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov
Details: Peskov said that strikes on Kyiv "are continuing regularly, in a targeted manner" and claimed they are "destroying military and military-adjacent infrastructure of the Kyiv regime".
Yet in recent weeks Russian strikes have been deliberately destroying warehouses in Ukraine that contain food, cosmetics, books and children's toys. In other words, Russia's attacks continue to target civilian infrastructure.
Peskov was also asked to comment on reports that Russia is preparing to escalate the conflict.
Quote: "As for escalation, well, those are the usual scare stories, plenty of which get published in Western media. We are continuing the special military operation, and the advance on the fronts is in fact obvious. It's obvious, and the experts understand perfectly well what this dynamic means and what consequences it ultimately has for the Kyiv regime."
More details: Peskov also said the issue of peace talks is on hold.
He claimed there are "no new ideas whatsoever" and that Ukraine "knows perfectly well what Russia's demands are".
Quote: "They don't want to discuss this through peaceful means. So we're continuing to maintain this dynamic, which is positive for us. And the operation goes on."
Background:
- Pyotr Tolstoy, Deputy Chairman of the State Duma (the lower chamber of the Russian parliament), has said Russia should openly bomb Ukrainian cities to demoralise the population and force Ukrainians to surrender to Russian troops "with their hands up".
- Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi declared that Tolstoy's calls to bomb Ukrainian cities should serve as grounds for an arrest warrant to be issued by the International Criminal Court. He said the only reason for Ukrainians to raise their hands is to "give Tolstoy and his fellow war criminals the middle finger".
- On 27 August, Russian propaganda claimed for the second time that a village in Sumy Oblast had been "liberated", only for Ukraine's Kursk Group of Forces to expose the lie being spread by the Russian military.

articles.title: American warship opens fire with new gun in Indian ocean
articles.body:
U.S. Navy destroyer USS Mustin has fired its recently installed Mark 38 Mod 4 30mm weapon during a live-fire exercise in the Indian Ocean, continuing operational use of the system after the ship became the first Arleigh Burke-class destroyer fitted with the new variant, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Images released by the U.S. Navy show the Mark 38 Mod 4 being fired from Mustin while the destroyer was underway in the Indian Ocean in August. The U.S. Navy identified the weapon as a 30mm machine gun and described the firing as part of a live-fire exercise.
Mustin, hull number DDG-89, is a Flight IIA Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer equipped with the Aegis combat system. The ship is currently forward-deployed and assigned to Destroyer Squadron 15, the principal surface force of the U.S. Navy’s 7th Fleet.
The Indian Ocean firing follows an earlier live-fire event involving the same weapon in the South China Sea on 17 April 2026. Mustin was the first destroyer of the Arleigh Burke class to receive the Mark 38 Mod 4, introducing the 30mm version of a weapon family already widely used aboard U.S. Navy surface ships.
The Mod 4 represents a change from earlier Mark 38 installations, which have generally been centred on a 25mm weapon. The newer configuration uses a 30mm gun, increasing the calibre available to ships for close-range engagements while retaining the remotely operated mounting concept used by the Mark 38 family.
Its installation aboard an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer gives the Navy another close-range gun option alongside the ship’s other defensive and offensive systems. The class typically carries the 5-inch Mk 45 naval gun, vertical launch cells for a range of missiles, Phalanx close-in weapon systems on relevant configurations, and smaller crew-served weapons.
Mustin was commissioned in July 2003 and was built by Ingalls Shipbuilding in Pascagoula, Mississippi. The destroyer previously spent an extended period forward-deployed in Japan and has operated regularly across the Western Pacific, including through the Taiwan Strait and in the South China Sea.
In May 2020, the ship conducted a freedom of navigation operation near the Paracel Islands, while in December of that year it transited the Taiwan Strait. The destroyer also attracted attention in 2021 while monitoring the Chinese aircraft carrier Liaoning and its accompanying surface ships in the region.
Mustin later shifted its homeport from Yokosuka to San Diego in 2021. The destroyer has since returned to forward-deployed operations in the U.S. 7th Fleet area, with the Navy identifying it in August as part of Destroyer Squadron 15.
Destroyer Squadron 15 is based in Japan and forms a major component of the U.S. Navy’s permanently forward-deployed surface force in the Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: As Iran Threatens Radio Farda And Other Media, US Points To Tehran's Record Of Targeting Journalists
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- The United States said it was aware of threats by Iran's armed forces to put Persian-language media outlets including RFE/RL's Radio Farda on a list of potential military targets, and pointed to what it said was Tehran's record of harassment and attempted attacks against journalists and dissidents abroad.
In an August 28 response to a query from RFE/RL, a State Department spokesperson said, "We are aware of these reports."
"The Iranian regime has repeatedly harassed and attempted to kidnap and kill journalists and Iranian dissidents worldwide simply for exercising their freedoms. This is longstanding, despicable behavior from a regime that has propagated terror globally for decades," the spokesperson said.
"The United States stands with innocent civilians targeted by Iran and continues working with allies and partners to expose these threats, share threat information, and hold perpetrators accountable," the spokesperson continued.
In a televised interview earlier this week, Iranian armed forces spokesman Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi named Radio Farda, Iran International, BBC Persian, and Manoto, and said their employees could be included in Iran's "bank of military targets." He called them "soldiers of Zionism and criminal America" and claimed, without providing evidence, that the outlets were connected variously to the CIA, Mossad, and other foreign intelligence services.
David Kramer, executive director of the George W. Bush Institute and a former US assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights, and labor, said Tehran's warning reflected the importance of the media outlets it said could be targeted.
"It's not a surprise that the Iranian regime would view outlets like Radio Farda and BBC Persian-language service as threats, since they don't want the Iranian people to know what's really happening," Kramer told RFE/RL.
"The regime's reaction shows that these services have a real impact inside Iran, whereas the regime prefers to operate through silence and violence against its own people and its neighbors," he said.
Radio Farda is the Iranian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), which says its mission is to "promote democratic values by providing accurate, uncensored news and open debate in countries where a free press is threatened and disinformation is pervasive."
Kramer said the media outlets "must be protected to be able to do their important work in advancing the interests of the American people through soft power, while also letting the Iranian people know they are not forgotten."
The Czech Republic, which hosts RFE/RL and Radio Farda in Prague, has protested the threats. Foreign Minister Petr Macinka said he was summoning the Iranian ambassador to appear at the ministry over the matter, Czech media reported.
"Radio Farda, based in Prague, has been one of the few channels getting verified information to the Iranian population. Its importance was especially clear during the mass repression which the Iranian regime subjected its people to in the winter," Czech Foreign Ministry spokesman Adam Corgo told Czech Radio.
He was referring to a deadly crackdown on nationwide protests in Iran in January. Foreign-based Iranian rights groups say they have verified around 7,000 deaths but that the real death toll is likely higher.
Thomas Melia, a former senior State Department official focusing on human rights and now a senior fellow at Georgetown University's Center for Democracy and Civil Society, said the threat should be taken seriously. He said Radio Farda personnel in Prague and elsewhere "need to heighten their security awareness," pointing to the Iranian state's actions targeting dissidents abroad.
Melia also said Tehran's threat underscored the importance of Radio Farda's work.
"It's a sign of how important the work of Farda is, that the Iranian regime is unhappy that the true facts and information and news reports that Farda broadcasts are getting to the Iranian people, and they want to cut that off," Melia said.
Christopher Walker, vice president of the Washington-based Center for European Policy Analysis, said Iran takes the competition over information seriously and has invested heavily in its state information capabilities.
"The Iranian authorities take media and information competition very seriously," Walker said. "It's why they are understood to spend hundreds of millions of dollars annually on their state information capabilities around the world."
Walker described the threats against international Persian-language outlets and other independent sources as part of what he called Tehran's "longstanding pattern of transnational censorship and repression."
He also placed the Iranian threats within a broader confrontation over information between authoritarian governments and Western democracies.
"This is part of a global shadow war being waged on the West by regimes in Moscow, Beijing, as well as Tehran," Walker said, to which "free countries need a far more cohesive and determined response."
Retired Vice Admiral Robert Harward, a former deputy commander of US Central Command, said Iran's hostility toward independent media was rooted in the nature of the clerical authorities who have held power since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
"At its core, the regime has always been against free press and anybody willing to speak, and they've been able to control that internally," Harward told RFE/RL. "Now, as they get more desperate, they're going to go after all the external pressure because it tells the truth about what a despotic regime it is," he said.
RFE/RL reports in 24 languages to 18 countries. It is a private, nonprofit American media corporation funded by a grant from the US Congress through the United States Agency for Global Media.
